renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is the dominant force driving filtration, opposed by capsular hydrostatic pressure and capillary oncotic pressure.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Constriction of the afferent arteriole has what effect on GFR and renal blood flow?
o: Decreases GFR but increases renal blood flow
Increases both GFR and renal blood flow
Increases GFR but decreases renal blood flow
Decreases both GFR and renal blood flow
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Afferent arteriolar constriction reduces glomerular capillary pressure, decreasing both GFR and renal plasma flow.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Mild constriction of the efferent arteriole typically has what effect on GFR?
o: Effect depends only on renal blood flow, not GFR
Increases GFR (by raising glomerular capillary pressure)
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Mild efferent constriction increases glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, transiently increasing GFR, though renal blood flow falls.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: The majority of filtered sodium, water, glucose, and amino acids are reabsorbed in which segment of the nephron?
o: Loop of Henle thick ascending limb
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the bulk (about two-thirds) of filtered sodium, water, glucose, and amino acids.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule occurs primarily via which transporter?
o: SGLT2 (and SGLT1) on the apical membrane, sodium-coupled
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: SGLT2 (proximal tubule) and SGLT1 (later segment) mediate sodium-glucose cotransport for glucose reabsorption.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: The renal threshold for glucose reabsorption, above which glucose appears in urine, is exceeded in which common clinical condition?
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: When plasma glucose exceeds the tubular transport maximum (Tm) for glucose, as in uncontrolled diabetes, glucosuria results.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is impermeable to water and actively reabsorbs which ions via the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter?
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: The NKCC2 cotransporter in the thick ascending limb reabsorbs sodium, potassium, and two chloride ions, driving the countercurrent multiplier and diluting tubular fluid.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which diuretic class acts on the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb?
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Loop diuretics inhibit the NKCC2 transporter in the thick ascending limb, producing potent diuresis.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Aldosterone acts primarily on which part of the nephron to increase sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion?
o: Loop of Henle thick ascending limb
Distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct (principal cells)
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Aldosterone acts on principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct, upregulating ENaC and Na-K-ATPase activity.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin) increases water permeability of the collecting duct by inserting which channel into the apical membrane?
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: ADH binds V2 receptors, triggering insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane of collecting duct principal cells.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: The countercurrent multiplier system in the loop of Henle establishes which physiological gradient?
o: A cortex-to-medulla increasing osmotic gradient, enabling urine concentration
A gradient that only affects potassium handling
A uniform osmolarity throughout the medulla
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: The countercurrent multiplier establishes a corticomedullary osmotic gradient (increasing toward the papilla), essential for concentrating urine.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Renal clearance of a substance that is freely filtered but also completely reabsorbed, with no secretion, would have a clearance value of approximately what?
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: A substance that is completely reabsorbed after filtration, with no secretion, has essentially zero clearance (e.g., glucose under normal conditions).

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) clearance is used to estimate which renal parameter, since it is both filtered and almost completely secreted?
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Because PAH is nearly completely cleared from plasma in a single pass (filtered plus secreted), its clearance approximates effective renal plasma flow.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Filtration fraction is defined as which ratio?
o: Urine flow rate divided by GFR
Renal plasma flow divided by GFR
GFR divided by renal plasma flow
Renal blood flow divided by cardiac output
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Filtration fraction = GFR / renal plasma flow, normally about 20%, representing the fraction of plasma flowing through the glomerulus that is filtered.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Autoregulation of renal blood flow and GFR is maintained across a range of arterial pressures primarily through which two mechanisms?
o: Sympathetic reflex and hormonal control only
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: The myogenic response (smooth muscle stretch-induced constriction) and tubuloglomerular feedback (via the macula densa) maintain renal autoregulation.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Tubuloglomerular feedback describes the mechanism by which increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa causes what effect?
o: No change in afferent arteriolar tone
Constriction of the afferent arteriole, decreasing GFR
Increased renin secretion and increased GFR
Dilation of the afferent arteriole, increasing GFR
Direct constriction of the efferent arteriole only
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Increased distal NaCl delivery triggers macula densa signaling that constricts the afferent arteriole, reducing GFR to protect against excessive filtration.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which hormone, secreted by juxtaglomerular cells in response to decreased renal perfusion pressure, initiates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system?
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Renin, released from juxtaglomerular cells in response to reduced perfusion pressure, cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, initiating the cascade.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), released in response to atrial stretch, has which overall effect on renal sodium and water handling?
o: Promotes natriuresis and diuresis (increased sodium and water excretion)
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: ANP promotes natriuresis and diuresis, opposing the RAAS, and helps regulate blood volume and pressure.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which segment of the nephron is the primary site of action for thiazide diuretics?
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Thiazides inhibit the Na-Cl cotransporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone act by which mechanism?
o: Antagonizing aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct
Osmotically drawing water into the tubule
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Spironolactone is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, reducing sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the collecting duct.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, such as acetazolamide, primarily reduce reabsorption of which ion in the proximal tubule?
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors block bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, causing bicarbonaturia and mild diuresis.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which of the following best describes the concept of renal 'plasma clearance' of a substance?
o: The concentration of the substance in urine only
The rate of glomerular filtration exclusively
The volume of blood completely cleared of the substance per unit time
The volume of plasma completely cleared of the substance per unit time
The total mass of substance excreted per day
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Clearance is defined as the volume of plasma from which a substance is completely removed (cleared) per unit time by the kidneys.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which of the following would most likely increase glomerular filtration rate acutely?
o: Dilation of the afferent arteriole and/or mild constriction of the efferent arteriole
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Afferent arteriolar dilation or mild efferent constriction both increase glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, raising GFR.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: The osmotic diuretic mannitol increases urine output primarily through which mechanism?
o: Increasing tubular fluid osmolarity, reducing water reabsorption
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Mannitol is freely filtered but poorly reabsorbed, raising tubular fluid osmolarity and thereby limiting passive water reabsorption.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which of the following substances undergoes significant tubular secretion, making its clearance exceed GFR?
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: PAH is both filtered and actively secreted by the proximal tubule, giving it a clearance close to total renal plasma flow, exceeding GFR.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which mechanism explains why plasma creatinine roughly doubles when GFR falls by about 50%?
o: Creatinine production doubles when GFR falls
A linear relationship between creatinine and GFR
Creatinine secretion increases proportionally with GFR decline
An inverse, roughly hyperbolic relationship between creatinine and GFR
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: The relationship between serum creatinine and GFR is inverse and hyperbolic; early GFR loss causes only modest creatinine rise, while further loss steeply raises creatinine.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which factor primarily determines the tubular maximum (Tm) for actively transported substances like glucose?
o: The number and saturation of available carrier transport proteins
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Tm reflects the saturation point of carrier-mediated transport systems; once transporters are saturated, additional filtered substance is excreted.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which of the following statements about the proximal tubule's reabsorption of bicarbonate is correct?
o: Filtered bicarbonate combines with secreted H+ to form carbonic acid, which is converted to CO2 and water, then CO2 diffuses in and reforms bicarbonate intracellularly
Bicarbonate reabsorption is independent of carbonic anhydrase
Bicarbonate is actively secreted rather than reabsorbed here
Bicarbonate is reabsorbed directly as bicarbonate ion across the apical membrane
Bicarbonate is not reabsorbed in the proximal tubule at all
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Proximal tubule bicarbonate reabsorption relies on luminal and intracellular carbonic anhydrase converting bicarbonate to CO2, which diffuses into the cell and is reconverted to bicarbonate for basolateral transport.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which nephron segment has the highest capacity for actively secreting hydrogen ions to acidify urine maximally, aided by intercalated cells?
o: Loop of Henle thin ascending limb
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Intercalated cells of the collecting duct actively secrete H+ (via H+-ATPase) against a steep gradient, allowing maximal urine acidification.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which of the following best describes the role of the vasa recta in maintaining the medullary osmotic gradient?
o: They actively pump solutes to maintain the gradient
They transport urine directly to the renal pelvis
They are the primary site of active sodium reabsorption
They have no role in the medullary gradient
They act as countercurrent exchangers, passively preserving the gradient by minimal net solute removal
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Vasa recta function as passive countercurrent exchangers, allowing blood flow through the medulla without washing out the osmotic gradient.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which of the following best explains why plasma proteins are normally largely excluded from the glomerular filtrate?
o: Binding to red blood cells preventing filtration
Active secretion back into the blood
Their large size and negative charge, repelled by the negatively charged basement membrane
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Size restriction and the negatively charged glomerular basement membrane and podocyte slit diaphragm restrict filtration of large, negatively charged plasma proteins like albumin.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which of the following would be expected to increase the filtration fraction?
o: Efferent arteriolar constriction (raising GFR relative to renal plasma flow)
Dilation of both afferent and efferent arterioles equally
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Efferent constriction raises GFR while reducing renal plasma flow, increasing the filtration fraction (GFR/RPF).

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which nephron segment is primarily responsible for diluting tubular fluid by reabsorbing solute without water, contributing to the ability to excrete free water?
o: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
Collecting duct in the presence of ADH
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: The water-impermeable thick ascending limb reabsorbs NaCl without water, diluting tubular fluid and enabling free water excretion when ADH is low.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which of the following would shift the tubular maximum (Tm) for glucose reabsorption to be exceeded at a lower plasma glucose level than normal?
o: A genetic reduction in the number of functional SGLT2 transporters (as in familial renal glucosuria)
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Reduced numbers or function of SGLT2 transporters lowers the effective Tm for glucose, causing glucosuria at normal or even low plasma glucose levels.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which of the following statements about the proximal tubule's handling of amino acids and glucose is correct?
o: Only glucose is reabsorbed; amino acids are fully excreted
Both are actively secreted rather than reabsorbed
Reabsorption of both is independent of sodium gradients
Both are reabsorbed almost completely via sodium-coupled cotransport under normal conditions
Neither is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Under normal physiological conditions, essentially all filtered glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed in the proximal tubule via sodium-dependent cotransporters.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which effect does prostaglandin E2 have on the renal vasculature, particularly relevant when NSAIDs are administered?
o: It causes vasoconstriction of afferent arterioles, protecting GFR
It causes vasodilation of afferent arterioles, helping maintain GFR especially when renal perfusion is compromised
It has no effect on renal blood flow
It directly increases sodium reabsorption only
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Renal prostaglandins (like PGE2) vasodilate the afferent arteriole, helping preserve GFR during states of reduced renal perfusion; NSAIDs blocking this can precipitate acute kidney injury.

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.s: Which of the following best describes autoregulation of GFR across a mean arterial pressure range of approximately 80-180 mmHg?
o: GFR remains relatively constant despite changes in arterial pressure within this range
GFR falls to zero below 180 mmHg
Autoregulation requires intact sympathetic innervation to function at all
Autoregulation only affects renal blood flow, never GFR
GFR varies linearly with arterial pressure across this range
renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.e: Renal autoregulation (myogenic and tubuloglomerular feedback mechanisms) maintains relatively stable GFR and renal blood flow across a wide range of arterial pressures.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: The normal arterial blood pH range is approximately what?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Normal arterial pH is tightly regulated between approximately 7.35 and 7.45.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which buffer system is the most important extracellular buffer in the blood?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: The bicarbonate-carbonic acid system is the primary extracellular buffer, described by the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: According to the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, pH is primarily determined by the ratio of which two variables?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3-]/(0.03 x PaCO2)), so pH depends on the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved CO2.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: A primary decrease in plasma bicarbonate with an appropriate compensatory decrease in PaCO2 describes which acid-base disorder?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Primary metabolic acidosis (low HCO3-) triggers compensatory hyperventilation, lowering PaCO2 to partially normalize pH.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which renal mechanism is the primary means of long-term compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis?
o: Increased renal bicarbonate reabsorption and new bicarbonate generation
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: In chronic respiratory acidosis, the kidneys increase bicarbonate reabsorption and generate new bicarbonate via increased ammoniagenesis and titratable acid excretion.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: The anion gap is calculated using which formula?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Anion gap = [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]), normally about 8-12 mEq/L, reflecting unmeasured anions.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: A high anion gap metabolic acidosis is characteristic of which condition?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: DKA generates ketoacids (unmeasured anions), widening the anion gap; diarrhea and RTA typically cause normal (hyperchloremic) anion gap acidosis.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which condition classically causes a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis due to bicarbonate loss from the gut?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Diarrhea causes loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid, leading to normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with compensatory hyperchloremia.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Renal tubular acidosis (RTA) type 1 (distal) results from impaired function of which process?
o: Impaired hydrogen ion secretion by intercalated cells of the collecting duct
Impaired sodium reabsorption in the loop of Henle
Impaired bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Distal (type 1) RTA results from an inability of intercalated cells to secrete hydrogen ions, impairing urinary acidification.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Renal tubular acidosis type 2 (proximal) results from impaired reabsorption of which substance in the proximal tubule?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Proximal (type 2) RTA results from defective bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, causing bicarbonate wasting.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Type 4 renal tubular acidosis is most commonly associated with which underlying hormonal abnormality?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Type 4 RTA results from hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance, causing hyperkalemia and impaired ammoniagenesis, leading to mild metabolic acidosis.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which mechanism allows the kidney to excrete excess hydrogen ions bound to a buffer, forming titratable acid, most commonly using which buffer?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Titratable acid excretion primarily involves hydrogen ions binding to filtered phosphate buffer in the tubular lumen.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Ammonia (NH3) produced by renal tubular cells combines with secreted hydrogen ions to form which excreted product?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Ammonia combines with H+ in the tubular lumen to form ammonium, which is excreted, allowing additional acid excretion without further lowering urine pH.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Chronic kidney disease commonly leads to metabolic acidosis due to which primary mechanism?
o: Reduced ability to excrete the daily acid load (reduced ammoniagenesis and acid excretion)
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: As nephron mass declines in CKD, the kidney's capacity to generate new bicarbonate and excrete the daily fixed acid load diminishes, causing metabolic acidosis.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which acid-base disturbance results from prolonged vomiting, due to loss of gastric hydrochloric acid?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Loss of hydrogen and chloride ions via vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis, often with a paradoxical aciduria due to volume depletion-driven aldosterone effects.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which compensatory respiratory response occurs in metabolic alkalosis?
o: Increased renal bicarbonate excretion only, no respiratory change
Hypoventilation, increasing PaCO2 to partially compensate
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: In metabolic alkalosis, respiratory compensation involves mild hypoventilation, raising PaCO2 to partially offset the elevated pH.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Winter's formula is used to calculate the expected compensatory PaCO2 in which primary acid-base disorder?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Winter's formula (PaCO2 = 1.5 x [HCO3-] + 8 ± 2) predicts appropriate respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with CO2 retention classically produces which primary acid-base disturbance?
o: Respiratory acidosis with renal metabolic compensation (elevated bicarbonate)
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Chronic hypoventilation causes CO2 retention (respiratory acidosis), with renal compensation raising bicarbonate over days.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Salicylate (aspirin) overdose classically produces which characteristic mixed acid-base disturbance?
o: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis only
Combined respiratory alkalosis (early, from direct respiratory center stimulation) and high anion gap metabolic acidosis
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Salicylates directly stimulate the respiratory center (causing early respiratory alkalosis) while also causing an anion gap metabolic acidosis from salicylate accumulation and interference with metabolism.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following best explains why hyperkalemia commonly accompanies metabolic acidosis?
o: Aldosterone secretion increases dramatically in acidosis, raising potassium
Acidosis has no effect on potassium distribution
Renal potassium reabsorption increases in acidosis
Hydrogen ions shift into cells in exchange for potassium moving out, raising serum potassium
Acidosis directly destroys red blood cells, releasing potassium
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: In acidosis, extracellular hydrogen ions are buffered intracellularly in exchange for potassium efflux, raising serum potassium levels.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following conditions is a classic cause of respiratory alkalosis due to hyperventilation?
o: Guillain-Barre syndrome with respiratory muscle weakness
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Anxiety-induced hyperventilation is a common cause of acute respiratory alkalosis, lowering PaCO2.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following best describes 'contraction alkalosis' seen with diuretic use or volume loss?
o: No relationship between fluid loss and acid-base status
Loss of bicarbonate-rich fluid, causing acidosis
Direct addition of bicarbonate to plasma
Loss of a bicarbonate-free fluid, concentrating the remaining bicarbonate and raising its plasma concentration
Increased renal bicarbonate excretion causing alkalosis
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Loss of extracellular fluid volume without proportional bicarbonate loss concentrates plasma bicarbonate, contributing to contraction alkalosis, often perpetuated by aldosterone-driven H+ secretion.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Renal compensation for a chronic primary respiratory alkalosis (e.g., living at high altitude) involves which mechanism?
o: Increased renal ammonia production, raising bicarbonate
Increased renal bicarbonate excretion, lowering plasma bicarbonate
Increased renal bicarbonate reabsorption, raising plasma bicarbonate
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Chronic respiratory alkalosis triggers renal excretion of bicarbonate to lower plasma pH toward normal over days.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following laboratory patterns would be expected in a patient with chronic renal failure and associated metabolic acidosis?
o: Low bicarbonate, low to normal pH, compensatory low PaCO2
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: CKD-associated metabolic acidosis presents with reduced bicarbonate, low-normal pH, and compensatory hyperventilation lowering PaCO2.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: A delta gap or delta ratio is used clinically to detect which additional acid-base abnormality in the setting of a high anion gap metabolic acidosis?
o: A coexisting normal anion gap metabolic acidosis or metabolic alkalosis
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: The delta gap/ratio helps identify whether a mixed acid-base disorder (e.g., concurrent normal anion gap acidosis or metabolic alkalosis) coexists with a high anion gap acidosis.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following statements about bicarbonate handling by the kidney is correct under normal conditions?
o: Bicarbonate reabsorption occurs mainly in the collecting duct
Most filtered bicarbonate is excreted in urine
Nearly all filtered bicarbonate is reabsorbed, primarily in the proximal tubule
Bicarbonate reabsorption is independent of hydrogen ion secretion
Bicarbonate is not filtered by the glomerulus
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Approximately 80-90% of filtered bicarbonate is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, coupled to hydrogen ion secretion.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which acid-base disorder would be expected in a patient with severe, prolonged vomiting who becomes significantly volume-depleted?
o: Metabolic alkalosis, potentially with paradoxical aciduria
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Vomiting causes loss of HCl, generating metabolic alkalosis; ongoing volume depletion perpetuates it via aldosterone-mediated renal H+ and K+ loss, sometimes causing paradoxical aciduria.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following best describes the physiological rationale for using bicarbonate as the primary buffer measured in arterial blood gas interpretation?
o: Bicarbonate levels are unaffected by any organ system
It is the only buffer present in blood
Bicarbonate is not clinically relevant to acid-base status
Its concentration can be easily calculated from pH and PaCO2 using the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship, and the lungs and kidneys can independently regulate its two components
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: The bicarbonate buffer system is an 'open system' where the respiratory system controls PaCO2 and the kidneys control bicarbonate, allowing independent physiological regulation and straightforward calculation via Henderson-Hasselbalch.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following best describes the expected primary acid-base disturbance in a patient with severe, prolonged diarrhea?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Diarrhea causes loss of bicarbonate-rich fluid from the lower GI tract, producing a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following best explains the mechanism of urinary buffering by phosphate, allowing continued hydrogen ion excretion even as urine pH falls?
o: Phosphate has no buffering capacity in urine
Phosphate is reabsorbed completely, preventing any buffering
Phosphate buffering only occurs in the blood, not urine
Filtered phosphate (HPO4^2-) accepts secreted hydrogen ions to form H2PO4-, which is excreted as titratable acid
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Filtered phosphate acts as a urinary buffer, accepting secreted H+ to form titratable acid, allowing ongoing acid excretion without further lowering urine pH.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: A patient with chronic vomiting and resultant hypokalemia develops paradoxical aciduria despite systemic alkalosis. Which mechanism explains this?
o: Direct renal excretion of excess acid from vomiting
Aldosterone-driven distal H+ secretion (to conserve sodium in states of volume depletion) despite systemic alkalosis
Increased bicarbonate excretion by the kidney
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Volume depletion from vomiting activates aldosterone, promoting distal sodium reabsorption coupled with hydrogen and potassium secretion, producing paradoxically acidic urine despite systemic alkalosis.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following acid-base disorders would be expected in a patient who is intentionally hyperventilating at high altitude to compensate for hypoxia?
o: Acute respiratory alkalosis, with renal compensation developing over days
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Hyperventilation-induced hypocapnia at altitude causes acute respiratory alkalosis, with renal bicarbonate excretion providing compensation over subsequent days.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following best describes the effect of chronic metabolic acidosis on bone in patients with advanced CKD?
o: Buffering of excess hydrogen ions by bone mineral, contributing to bone demineralization over time
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Chronic acidosis can be buffered in part by bone, which releases alkaline salts, potentially contributing to bone demineralization in CKD.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following would most likely be seen on arterial blood gas analysis in a patient with acute severe asthma exacerbation with worsening fatigue?
o: No change in PaCO2 at any stage
Initial respiratory alkalosis progressing to respiratory acidosis as fatigue develops
Immediate respiratory acidosis without an initial alkalotic phase
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Early asthma exacerbations often show hyperventilation-driven respiratory alkalosis; as respiratory muscle fatigue develops, CO2 retention causes a shift toward respiratory acidosis, a worrying sign.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following best explains why patients with chronic renal failure often have both metabolic acidosis and hyperkalemia?
o: CKD causes exclusively potassium problems, not acid-base problems
Reduced nephron mass impairs both acid excretion (ammoniagenesis) and potassium excretion
These two abnormalities are unrelated in CKD
Aldosterone excess in CKD causes both problems
Acidosis causes potassium to move into cells, worsening hyperkalemia
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Progressive nephron loss impairs both the kidney's capacity to excrete the daily acid load and to secrete potassium, contributing to concurrent acidosis and hyperkalemia; acidosis further shifts potassium out of cells, compounding hyperkalemia.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which condition is a recognized cause of a high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to accumulation of lactate?
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Tissue hypoperfusion in shock states leads to anaerobic metabolism and lactate accumulation, producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following is the expected compensatory response to a primary metabolic alkalosis, according to normal physiological limits?
o: Renal bicarbonate reabsorption increases further, worsening the alkalosis without limit
PaCO2 rises, but rarely above approximately 55 mmHg due to hypoxic drive limiting further hypoventilation
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Respiratory compensation for metabolic alkalosis is limited because significant hypoventilation would cause hypoxia, which stimulates ventilation, capping the compensatory rise in PaCO2.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following statements about mixed acid-base disorders is correct?
o: Mixed disorders are diagnosed by pH alone without considering PaCO2 or bicarbonate
Anion gap calculation is unnecessary in mixed disorders
Mixed disorders cannot occur; only one primary disorder can be present at a time
More than one primary acid-base disturbance can coexist, such as combined metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis in sepsis
Compensation always fully normalizes pH in mixed disorders
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Patients can have more than one primary acid-base disturbance simultaneously (e.g., sepsis causing both lactic acidosis and hyperventilation-driven respiratory alkalosis), requiring careful stepwise analysis.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which parameter, along with PaCO2 and bicarbonate, is essential to assess when interpreting an arterial blood gas for a mixed acid-base disorder?
o: The anion gap and clinical context
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Calculating the anion gap and considering clinical context alongside pH, PaCO2, and bicarbonate is essential for correctly identifying mixed acid-base disturbances.

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.s: Which of the following best describes 'appropriate' respiratory compensation for a primary metabolic disturbance?
o: The direction of PaCO2 change matches the primary disturbance to help normalize pH (e.g., PaCO2 falls in metabolic acidosis)
PaCO2 always moves in the same direction regardless of the primary disorder
Respiratory compensation always fully corrects pH to normal
Compensation occurs instantaneously in metabolic disorders
Compensation only occurs for respiratory primary disorders
renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.e: Appropriate compensation involves the secondary system moving in a direction that mitigates the pH change caused by the primary disorder, though it typically does not fully normalize pH.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: The kidney develops from which three successive embryological structures?
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: The kidney develops sequentially through pronephros (non-functional), mesonephros (transient), and metanephros (definitive adult kidney).

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: The definitive adult kidney (metanephros) arises from which two embryological components?
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: The ureteric bud (from the mesonephric duct) induces the metanephric mesenchyme, giving rise to the collecting system and nephrons respectively.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: The ureteric bud gives rise to which structures of the adult kidney?
o: Ureter, renal pelvis, calyces, and collecting ducts
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: The ureteric bud develops into the collecting duct system, calyces, renal pelvis, and ureter.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: The metanephric mesenchyme (blastema) differentiates into which nephron components?
o: Glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, and distal tubule
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: The metanephric mesenchyme forms the nephron proper, from Bowman's capsule through the distal convoluted tubule.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Renal agenesis, the complete absence of one or both kidneys, results from failure of which embryological event?
o: Failure of ureteric bud formation or its interaction with metanephric mesenchyme
Failure of the cloaca to divide
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Renal agenesis results from failure of the ureteric bud to form or to properly induce the metanephric mesenchyme.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Bilateral renal agenesis is classically associated with which severe fetal complication due to lack of fetal urine production?
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Fetal urine is a major contributor to amniotic fluid; bilateral renal agenesis causes severe oligohydramnios, leading to Potter sequence with pulmonary hypoplasia.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: The glomerular filtration barrier consists of which three layers?
o: Simple squamous epithelium, smooth muscle, and connective tissue
Fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane, and podocyte foot processes with filtration slits
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: The filtration barrier comprises fenestrated capillary endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane, and podocyte foot processes forming filtration slits.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Podocytes are specialized epithelial cells whose foot processes interdigitate to form which structure important for filtration?
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Podocyte foot processes create filtration slits bridged by slit diaphragms, forming the final barrier to protein filtration.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Mesangial cells, located between glomerular capillaries, perform which functions?
o: Structural support, phagocytosis of debris, and contractile regulation of capillary flow
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Mesangial cells provide structural support, phagocytose trapped macromolecules, and can contract to regulate glomerular capillary surface area and flow.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which histological cell type lines the proximal convoluted tubule, characterized by a prominent brush border?
o: Simple cuboidal cells with microvilli (brush border)
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Proximal tubule cells are simple cuboidal with an extensive apical brush border, maximizing reabsorptive surface area.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: The thin segments of the loop of Henle are lined by which epithelial type?
o: Simple cuboidal epithelium with brush border
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: The thin descending and ascending limbs of the loop of Henle are lined by simple squamous epithelium, facilitating passive transport.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: The collecting duct contains two main cell types: principal cells and intercalated cells. What is the primary function of principal cells?
o: Sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion (regulated by aldosterone) and water reabsorption (regulated by ADH)
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Principal cells mediate sodium/water reabsorption and potassium secretion, regulated by aldosterone and ADH respectively.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Intercalated cells of the collecting duct are primarily responsible for which function?
o: Acid-base regulation via hydrogen ion or bicarbonate secretion
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Intercalated cells (type A and type B) regulate acid-base balance through H+ or HCO3- secretion respectively.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: The renal capsule is composed of which type of connective tissue?
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: The renal (fibrous) capsule is a tough layer of dense irregular connective tissue directly surrounding the kidney.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which epithelial type lines the ureter, renal pelvis, and bladder, allowing for distension?
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Transitional epithelium (urothelium) lines the urinary tract from the renal pelvis to the proximal urethra, allowing stretch without damage.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Posterior urethral valves, a congenital cause of obstructive uropathy in male infants, result from abnormal tissue in which location?
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Posterior urethral valves are abnormal mucosal folds in the posterior (prostatic) urethra causing bladder outlet obstruction in male infants.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which structure is the vestigial remnant of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct in females?
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Gartner's duct is the remnant of the regressed mesonephric duct along the lateral vaginal wall in females.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: In males, the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct persists and differentiates into which structures?
o: Epididymis, vas deferens, and seminal vesicle
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Under the influence of testosterone, the mesonephric duct differentiates into the epididymis, vas deferens, and seminal vesicle.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Multicystic dysplastic kidney differs from polycystic kidney disease in that it typically presents with which feature?
o: Progressive bilateral cystic enlargement with eventual renal failure in adulthood
Unilateral, non-functioning kidney with disorganized cysts, often an isolated developmental anomaly
Normal renal architecture with cysts only in the medulla
Bilateral, symmetric enlargement with function preserved
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Multicystic dysplastic kidney is typically a unilateral, sporadic developmental anomaly with disorganized dysplastic tissue and non-functioning parenchyma, unlike the inherited progressive polycystic kidney diseases.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which structure allows communication and induces reciprocal differentiation between the ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme during nephrogenesis?
o: Hormonal signals from the placenta exclusively
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Reciprocal inductive (paracrine) signaling between the ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme drives normal nephron and collecting duct development.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: At what approximate gestational age does nephrogenesis (formation of new nephrons) normally cease?
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Nephrogenesis is normally complete by approximately 34-36 weeks of gestation; preterm infants may be born with fewer nephrons.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which glomerular basement membrane component, when targeted by autoantibodies, causes Goodpasture syndrome?
o: Type IV collagen (alpha-3 chain, NC1 domain)
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Goodpasture syndrome involves autoantibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in the glomerular (and alveolar) basement membrane.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which structure connects the metanephric blastema-derived nephron to the ureteric bud-derived collecting duct, ensuring a continuous lumen for urine flow?
o: A direct fusion between the connecting tubule (nephron-derived) and the collecting duct (ureteric bud-derived)
No connection exists between the two structures normally
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: The connecting tubule, derived from the metanephric mesenchyme, fuses with the collecting duct system from the ureteric bud to establish tubular continuity.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which of the following histological findings is characteristic of minimal change disease when examined by electron microscopy?
o: Diffuse effacement (fusion) of podocyte foot processes with normal light microscopy appearance
Thickened glomerular basement membrane with immune complex deposits
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Minimal change disease characteristically shows diffuse podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy, with an essentially normal glomerulus on light microscopy.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which layer of the ureteric wall contains smooth muscle arranged to generate peristaltic contractions propelling urine toward the bladder?
o: Muscularis (inner longitudinal, outer circular, and in the lower third an additional outer longitudinal layer)
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: The muscularis layer of the ureter, with its longitudinal and circular smooth muscle, generates peristalsis to propel urine.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which term describes the histological finding of glomerular scarring/sclerosis affecting only a portion of glomeruli and a portion of each affected glomerulus, as seen in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis?
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis affects some (focal) glomeruli, and only a portion (segmental) of each affected glomerulus, as its name implies.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: The pronephros in humans is functionally significant in which way?
o: It is non-functional and regresses, though its duct may contribute to the mesonephric duct
It persists as the adult renal pelvis
It is the definitive functional kidney throughout life
It gives rise to the bladder
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: The human pronephros is vestigial and non-functional, regressing early, though associated duct structures contribute to later mesonephric duct development.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: The mesonephros functions transiently as an interim kidney during which developmental period, before regressing (except for genital duct derivatives)?
o: During early-to-mid fetal life, before the metanephros becomes functional
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: The mesonephros functions as a temporary excretory organ during fetal development before regressing, with its duct persisting as part of the male genital system.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which histological feature distinguishes the renal cortex from the medulla on light microscopy?
o: The medulla is composed only of connective tissue
The cortex has no tubular structures
The medulla contains glomeruli; the cortex does not
The cortex contains glomeruli and convoluted tubules; the medulla contains the loops of Henle and collecting ducts organized into pyramids
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: The renal cortex is characterized by the presence of glomeruli and convoluted tubules, whereas the medulla contains the loops of Henle, vasa recta, and collecting ducts forming pyramids.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Renal columns (of Bertin) refer to which anatomical feature seen on kidney sections?
o: A type of nephron unique to the medulla
A part of the collecting system only
Extensions of cortical tissue that dip between adjacent renal pyramids
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Renal columns are cortical tissue extending between the medullary pyramids, visible on gross and histological sections.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which structure represents the point of fusion between the ureteric bud-derived collecting duct and metanephric mesenchyme-derived nephron, critical for establishing continuous nephron drainage?
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Fusion at the connecting tubule ensures continuity between the nephron (mesenchymal origin) and the collecting duct system (ureteric bud origin).

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which of the following congenital anomalies results from persistence of fetal lobulations of the kidney into adulthood, generally without functional consequence?
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Persistent fetal lobation is a benign anatomical variant where the normal fetal lobulated contour of the kidney persists into adult life.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which cell type of the glomerulus is contractile and can regulate glomerular capillary surface area available for filtration, in addition to phagocytic functions?
o: Parietal epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Mesangial cells have contractile properties allowing regulation of capillary loop surface area, in addition to structural support and phagocytic clearance of debris.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Parietal epithelial cells lining Bowman's capsule are of which histological type?
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: The parietal layer of Bowman's capsule is lined by simple squamous epithelium, continuous with the visceral podocyte layer at the vascular pole.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which vascular structure is specifically found only in juxtamedullary nephrons and not cortical nephrons, aiding the countercurrent mechanism?
o: Long loops of Henle extending deep into the medulla with accompanying vasa recta
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Juxtamedullary nephrons uniquely have long loops of Henle penetrating deep into the medulla, paired with vasa recta, essential for the countercurrent multiplication and exchange systems.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which of the following describes the histological appearance of the macula densa cells within the distal tubule at the vascular pole?
o: Squamous cells with no specialized function
Cells identical to proximal tubule cells
Columnar cells with closely packed nuclei, specialized for sensing tubular fluid NaCl concentration
Cells forming part of the glomerular capillary wall
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Macula densa cells are specialized, closely packed columnar cells of the distal tubule that sense luminal NaCl concentration, forming part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus feedback loop.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which of the following statements correctly relates the ureteric bud's branching pattern to the number of nephrons formed?
o: The ureteric bud has no relationship to nephron number
Nephron number is fixed regardless of ureteric bud branching pattern
All nephrons form independently of ureteric bud branching
Only a single nephron forms from the entire ureteric bud
Each terminal branch of the ureteric bud induces formation of a nephron via reciprocal induction with surrounding mesenchyme
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Progressive branching of the ureteric bud induces the surrounding metanephric mesenchyme at each branch tip to form nephrons, so branching pattern strongly influences final nephron number.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Oligonephronia (a congenitally reduced nephron number, as seen in low-birth-weight or preterm infants) is associated with increased risk of which later-life condition?
o: Hypertension and chronic kidney disease in adulthood
Increased risk of renal cell carcinoma only
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Reduced nephron endowment at birth (oligonephronia) is associated with increased risk of hypertension and progressive chronic kidney disease later in life.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which of the following is the embryological origin of the trigone of the bladder, distinguishing its smooth-walled appearance from the rest of the bladder?
o: Cloacal endoderm exclusively, same as the rest of the bladder
Absorbed distal mesonephric ducts (of mesodermal origin), unlike the endodermal origin of the rest of the bladder
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: The trigone derives from absorbed mesonephric duct tissue (mesodermal), giving it a distinct smooth-walled histological appearance compared to the endoderm-derived remainder of the bladder.

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.s: Which of the following best describes the histological hallmark of diabetic nephropathy affecting the glomerulus, known as Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules?
o: Nodular glomerulosclerosis with mesangial matrix expansion
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.e: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules are characteristic nodular areas of mesangial matrix expansion and sclerosis seen in diabetic nephropathy.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Approximately what percentage of total body weight in an average adult male is composed of water?
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Total body water constitutes approximately 60% of body weight in adult males, with somewhat lower percentages in females due to higher fat content.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Of total body water, approximately what fraction is intracellular versus extracellular?
o: Equal distribution between the two compartments
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Approximately two-thirds of total body water is intracellular fluid, and one-third is extracellular (interstitial plus plasma).

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which ion is the primary determinant of extracellular fluid osmolarity?
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Sodium and its accompanying anions are the major determinants of extracellular osmolarity, given sodium's predominance in the ECF.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which hormone is the primary regulator of plasma osmolarity through its effect on renal water reabsorption?
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: ADH, released in response to increased plasma osmolarity (sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors), promotes water reabsorption in the collecting duct.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which hormone is the primary regulator of extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure through effects on sodium reabsorption?
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Aldosterone, via the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, regulates sodium (and thus volume) reabsorption in response to perceived volume status.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Erythropoietin, essential for red blood cell production, is produced primarily by which renal cell type?
o: Peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells in the renal cortex
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Erythropoietin is produced mainly by peritubular interstitial cells in the renal cortex in response to hypoxia.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Chronic kidney disease commonly leads to anemia primarily due to which mechanism?
o: Reduced erythropoietin production by damaged kidneys
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Progressive nephron loss reduces erythropoietin-producing capacity, leading to normocytic normochromic anemia in CKD.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: The kidney contributes to calcium homeostasis by converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active form. Which enzyme performs this conversion?
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to the active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol).

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Chronic kidney disease-mineral bone disorder (CKD-MBD) commonly results in which hormonal abnormality due to reduced calcitriol production and phosphate retention?
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Reduced calcitriol and phosphate retention in CKD lower serum calcium, stimulating compensatory (secondary) parathyroid hormone secretion.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Parathyroid hormone acts on the kidney to increase reabsorption of which ion and decrease reabsorption of which other ion?
o: Increases calcium reabsorption; decreases phosphate reabsorption
Increases both calcium and phosphate reabsorption
Increases phosphate reabsorption; decreases calcium reabsorption
Has no direct renal tubular effect
Decreases both calcium and phosphate reabsorption
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: PTH increases distal tubular calcium reabsorption while inhibiting proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption (phosphaturic effect).

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which electrolyte disturbance is most dangerous acutely due to its effect on cardiac conduction, often seen in acute kidney injury?
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Hyperkalemia can cause life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias and is a common, dangerous complication of acute kidney injury.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which ECG change is classically an early sign of hyperkalemia?
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Peaked T waves are an early ECG manifestation of hyperkalemia, progressing to widened QRS and eventual sine-wave pattern if untreated.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH) classically causes which electrolyte abnormality?
o: Hyponatremia with concentrated urine despite low plasma osmolarity
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Excess ADH causes water retention, diluting plasma sodium (hyponatremia) while urine remains inappropriately concentrated.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Diabetes insipidus, characterized by excretion of large volumes of dilute urine, results from deficiency or resistance to which hormone?
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Diabetes insipidus results from either inadequate ADH secretion (central) or renal resistance to ADH (nephrogenic), impairing water reabsorption.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Central diabetes insipidus differs from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus in its response to which diagnostic test?
o: Administration of desmopressin (DDAVP): central DI responds with urine concentration, nephrogenic DI does not
Water deprivation test alone, with no distinguishing feature
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Central DI (lacking ADH) responds to exogenous desmopressin with urine concentration, while nephrogenic DI (renal resistance to ADH) does not respond adequately.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following best describes the physiological trigger for thirst and ADH release?
o: Increased plasma osmolarity, sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect rising plasma osmolarity, triggering both thirst and ADH release to conserve water.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which condition results from severe hyponatremia being corrected too rapidly, causing a serious neurological complication?
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome, a serious and often irreversible neurological injury.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following is the primary physiological stimulus for aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex, aside from angiotensin II?
o: Hyperkalemia (direct stimulation of the zona glomerulosa)
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Elevated plasma potassium directly stimulates aldosterone secretion from the zona glomerulosa, promoting renal potassium excretion.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism by which angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors help manage fluid/electrolyte and blood pressure status in hypertension?
o: They prevent conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: ACE inhibitors block the conversion of angiotensin I to the potent vasoconstrictor and aldosterone-stimulating angiotensin II.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which laboratory finding is characteristic of primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome)?
o: Hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis with suppressed renin
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Excess aldosterone in Conn syndrome causes sodium retention (hypertension), potassium wasting (hypokalemia), and metabolic alkalosis, with renin suppressed due to volume expansion.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following best describes the third spacing of fluid, as seen in conditions like severe burns or nephrotic syndrome?
o: Normal redistribution of fluid during exercise
Fluid shift from intracellular to extracellular compartment
Fluid shift from extracellular to intracellular compartment
Pathological accumulation of fluid in a non-functional interstitial or body cavity space, reducing effective circulating volume
Fluid accumulation strictly within blood vessels
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Third spacing refers to fluid trapped in interstitial or cavity spaces (e.g., ascites, edema) that is not readily available to the functional circulating volume.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following electrolyte disturbances is classically associated with tetany, presenting with signs such as Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs?
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability, causing tetany, with Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs as classic clinical findings.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Renal handling of potassium primarily occurs through filtration and reabsorption in the proximal tubule and loop of Henle, with net excretion being regulated mainly at which site?
o: Distal tubule and collecting duct (principal cells, aldosterone-regulated)
Loop of Henle thin descending limb
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: While most filtered potassium is reabsorbed proximally, net urinary potassium excretion is finely regulated by principal cell secretion in the distal nephron and collecting duct, influenced by aldosterone.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following conditions would be expected to cause hypokalemia through renal potassium wasting?
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Excess aldosterone activity increases distal potassium secretion, leading to hypokalemia through renal wasting.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following would most directly stimulate renin release from juxtaglomerular cells?
o: Decreased renal perfusion pressure (sensed by afferent arteriolar baroreceptors)
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Reduced renal perfusion pressure, sensed by baroreceptors in the afferent arteriole, is a key stimulus for renin release, alongside sympathetic activation and macula densa signaling.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which compartment comprises the extracellular fluid, aside from plasma?
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Extracellular fluid consists of plasma and interstitial fluid, together comprising about one-third of total body water.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following would be the expected physiological response to a large water load in a healthy individual?
o: Increased ADH secretion, causing water retention
Decreased ADH secretion, leading to excretion of dilute urine
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: A water load dilutes plasma osmolarity, suppressing ADH release and allowing excretion of dilute urine to restore osmotic balance.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following would be expected in a patient with severe dehydration due to inadequate water intake?
o: Increased plasma osmolarity, increased ADH secretion, and concentrated urine
Decreased plasma osmolarity and decreased ADH
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Dehydration raises plasma osmolarity, stimulating both thirst and ADH release, resulting in concentrated urine to conserve water.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following hormones acts on bone and kidney to raise serum calcium, in part by stimulating osteoclastic bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption?
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: PTH raises serum calcium via bone resorption, increased renal tubular calcium reabsorption, and stimulation of renal calcitriol synthesis.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following would be the expected effect of chronic renal failure on serum phosphate levels, particularly in later stages?
o: Decreased serum phosphate due to increased renal clearance
No change in serum phosphate regardless of GFR
Decreased serum phosphate due to reduced intake
Phosphate levels are regulated independently of renal function
Increased serum phosphate (hyperphosphatemia) due to reduced renal excretion
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: As GFR declines in CKD, the kidney's capacity to excrete phosphate diminishes, leading to hyperphosphatemia, particularly in advanced stages.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following is a direct consequence of erythropoietin deficiency in advanced chronic kidney disease?
o: Microcytic hypochromic anemia primarily due to EPO deficiency alone
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Erythropoietin deficiency in CKD typically produces a normocytic, normochromic anemia due to reduced red cell production.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following statements about potassium homeostasis is correct regarding the relationship between insulin and cellular potassium uptake?
o: Insulin only affects glucose, not electrolyte handling
Insulin promotes intracellular potassium uptake via stimulation of the Na-K-ATPase pump, making it useful in treating acute hyperkalemia
Insulin has no effect on potassium distribution
Insulin promotes potassium release from cells
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Insulin stimulates the Na-K-ATPase pump, driving potassium into cells; this is exploited clinically (insulin plus glucose) as an emergency treatment to temporarily lower serum potassium in hyperkalemia.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following best explains the renal response to volume depletion in terms of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system?
o: Volume depletion has no effect on the RAAS
RAAS activation promotes sodium and water excretion in volume depletion
Decreased renal perfusion stimulates renin release, ultimately increasing aldosterone secretion and sodium/water retention
Aldosterone secretion decreases in volume depletion
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Volume depletion reduces renal perfusion pressure, triggering renin release and subsequent RAAS activation to restore volume via sodium and water retention.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following conditions would classically present with hypernatremia due to a pure water deficit, such as inadequate free access to water?
o: Diabetes insipidus with restricted water intake
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Diabetes insipidus causes excessive free water loss; if water intake cannot keep pace (e.g., in infants or altered mental status), hypernatremia results.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following describes the physiological role of natriuretic peptides (ANP and BNP) in cardiovascular and renal regulation?
o: They promote natriuresis, diuresis, and vasodilation, counter-regulating the RAAS
They promote sodium retention and vasoconstriction
They have no interaction with the RAAS
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Natriuretic peptides, released in response to atrial/ventricular stretch (volume overload), promote natriuresis, diuresis, and vasodilation, opposing RAAS effects.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following would be an expected laboratory finding in a patient with chronic kidney disease-related secondary hyperparathyroidism?
o: Normal PTH with abnormal calcium and phosphate
Low PTH, high calcium, low phosphate
Elevated PTH, low or low-normal calcium, elevated phosphate
Low PTH and low phosphate together
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD is characterized by elevated PTH in response to low calcitriol, low/low-normal calcium, and elevated phosphate from reduced renal clearance.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following would most directly result from long-standing untreated primary hyperparathyroidism affecting bone?
o: Osteitis fibrosa cystica due to excess osteoclastic bone resorption
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Chronic excess PTH drives osteoclastic bone resorption, potentially causing osteitis fibrosa cystica with characteristic brown tumors in severe, prolonged cases.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following best describes the role of aquaporin-1 channels in the proximal tubule?
o: They provide constitutive, ADH-independent water permeability for bulk isosmotic reabsorption
They are regulated by ADH for fine-tuning water reabsorption
They transport sodium rather than water
They are found only in the collecting duct
They actively transport water against its concentration gradient
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Aquaporin-1 channels in the proximal tubule and descending thin limb provide constitutive water permeability, independent of ADH regulation, supporting bulk isosmotic fluid reabsorption.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following electrolyte disturbances would be expected with the use of loop diuretics, given their site and mechanism of action?
o: Hypokalemia and hypercalciuria (increased urinary calcium loss)
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: Loop diuretics inhibit NKCC2, reducing the lumen-positive potential that drives paracellular calcium and magnesium reabsorption, causing hypercalciuria, alongside potassium wasting distally.

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.s: Which of the following would be an expected compensatory renal response to chronic metabolic alkalosis with adequate chloride and volume repletion?
o: Increased renal bicarbonate excretion, correcting the alkalosis
Continued renal bicarbonate retention, perpetuating the alkalosis
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.e: With adequate chloride and volume status, the kidney can effectively excrete excess bicarbonate, correcting a chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which lobe of the cerebrum contains the primary motor cortex?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus) is located in the frontal lobe.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The primary somatosensory cortex is located in which gyrus?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe houses the primary somatosensory cortex.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Broca's area, associated with speech production, is typically located in which lobe and hemisphere?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Broca's area, in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere, is essential for speech production; its damage causes expressive (non-fluent) aphasia.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Wernicke's area, associated with language comprehension, is located in which lobe?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Wernicke's area in the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere is crucial for language comprehension; damage causes fluent (receptive) aphasia.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The primary visual cortex is located in which lobe, around the calcarine sulcus?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The primary visual cortex (V1) surrounds the calcarine sulcus in the occipital lobe.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The thalamus functions primarily as which of the following?
o: A structure exclusively involved in vision
The primary site of memory consolidation
The site of voluntary motor initiation
A relay station for sensory (except olfactory) information to the cortex
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The thalamus relays nearly all sensory modalities (except olfaction) to the appropriate cortical areas.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which structure of the diencephalon regulates autonomic function, temperature, and the pituitary gland?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The hypothalamus is the master regulator of autonomic function, temperature, hunger, thirst, and pituitary hormone control.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The basal ganglia are primarily involved in which function?
o: Coordination and modulation of voluntary movement
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra) modulate voluntary movement initiation and control.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta is the hallmark pathology of which disease?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Parkinson's disease results from progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The cerebellum primarily functions to coordinate which of the following?
o: Balance, coordination, and fine-tuning of movement
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The cerebellum coordinates balance, posture, and fine motor control, comparing intended and actual movement.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Damage to the cerebellum classically produces which clinical sign?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, and other coordination deficits, typically ipsilateral to the lesion.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The midbrain contains which important structures related to eye movement and reflexes?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The midbrain's superior colliculi are involved in visual reflexes/eye movements, and inferior colliculi in auditory reflexes.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which cranial nerve nuclei are located in the pons?
o: CN V, VI, VII, and VIII (in part)
CN IX, X, XI, XII exclusively
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The pons houses nuclei for cranial nerves V (trigeminal), VI (abducens), VII (facial), and VIII (vestibulocochlear).

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which cranial nerves have their nuclei located in the medulla oblongata?
o: CN IX, X, XI, and XII
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The medulla contains nuclei for cranial nerves IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (accessory), and XII (hypoglossal).

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The corticospinal tract decussates (crosses to the opposite side) primarily at which level?
o: Pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Approximately 85-90% of corticospinal fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla, forming the lateral corticospinal tract.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The internal capsule is a critical white matter structure through which most cortical fibers pass; it lies between which two structures?
o: Thalamus and basal ganglia (caudate and lentiform nuclei)
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The internal capsule is a compact white matter tract situated between the thalamus/caudate nucleus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: A lacunar stroke affecting the posterior limb of the internal capsule classically presents with which clinical picture?
o: Pure motor hemiparesis contralateral to the lesion
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Lacunar infarcts in the posterior limb of the internal capsule classically cause pure motor hemiparesis, as descending corticospinal fibers are densely packed there.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The circle of Willis is formed by anastomoses between which major arterial systems?
o: Superior and inferior cerebellar arteries only
Anterior and posterior spinal arteries only
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The circle of Willis connects the internal carotid (anterior) and vertebrobasilar (posterior) circulations, providing collateral blood flow.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Occlusion of the middle cerebral artery classically causes contralateral weakness affecting which body regions most severely?
o: Upper limb and face more than lower limb
Lower limb more than upper limb and face
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The MCA supplies the lateral cerebral cortex, where the face and arm are more heavily represented on the motor homunculus, causing predominant face/arm weakness.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Occlusion of the anterior cerebral artery classically causes contralateral weakness affecting which body region most severely?
o: Lower limb (leg) more than face and arm
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The ACA supplies the medial cerebral cortex, where the leg is represented on the homunculus, causing predominant contralateral leg weakness.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The hippocampus, located in the medial temporal lobe, is primarily responsible for which cognitive function?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The hippocampus plays a crucial role in the consolidation of new explicit (declarative) memories.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Bilateral hippocampal damage classically results in which memory deficit, as seen in the famous patient H.M.?
o: Retrograde amnesia only, with intact new memory formation
Anterograde amnesia, impaired formation of new long-term memories
Complete loss of all memory including procedural skills
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Bilateral hippocampal damage classically causes anterograde amnesia, impairing the ability to form new declarative memories, while old memories and procedural learning may be preserved.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The amygdala is primarily associated with which of the following functions?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The amygdala plays a central role in processing fear and emotionally significant stimuli, and in emotional memory formation.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The corpus callosum primarily functions to do what?
o: Relay sensory information to the thalamus
Connect the cerebellum to the cerebrum
Connect the two cerebral hemispheres, allowing interhemispheric communication
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The corpus callosum is the largest commissure, connecting corresponding areas of the two cerebral hemispheres.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Damage to the reticular activating system in the brainstem classically results in which clinical state?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The reticular activating system maintains wakefulness and arousal; its disruption can result in decreased consciousness or coma.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which ventricle is located within the cerebral hemispheres, one on each side?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The paired lateral ventricles are located within each cerebral hemisphere, connecting to the third ventricle via the interventricular foramina (of Monro).
