nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Cerebrospinal fluid is primarily produced by which structure?
o: Ependymal cells alone without choroid plexus contribution
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The choroid plexus, found in the ventricles, is the primary site of CSF production.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: CSF is reabsorbed into the venous system primarily via which structure?
o: Central canal of the spinal cord
Arachnoid villi/granulations into the dural venous sinuses
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Arachnoid granulations project into the dural venous sinuses (especially superior sagittal sinus), allowing CSF reabsorption into venous blood.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) causes which type of hydrocephalus?
o: Normal pressure hydrocephalus only in adults
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Aqueductal stenosis blocks CSF flow between the third and fourth ventricles, causing non-communicating hydrocephalus with dilation proximal to the obstruction.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The blood-brain barrier is formed primarily by which structural feature of cerebral capillaries?
o: Tight junctions between endothelial cells, supported by astrocytic end-feet
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Tight junctions between cerebral capillary endothelial cells, along with astrocytic foot process support, form the selective blood-brain barrier.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which of the following brain regions lacks a complete blood-brain barrier, allowing sensing of blood-borne substances (as in the area postrema, involved in vomiting)?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Circumventricular organs, including the area postrema, lack a complete blood-brain barrier, allowing direct sensing of blood composition.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The limbic system, involved in emotion and memory, includes which of the following key structures?
o: Hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, and hypothalamus
Primary visual and auditory cortices exclusively
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The limbic system encompasses interconnected structures including the hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, and hypothalamus, central to emotion and memory.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which artery supplies the primary visual cortex, making its occlusion a cause of contralateral homonymous hemianopia often with macular sparing?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital lobe including the visual cortex; occlusion causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing due to collateral MCA supply.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which lobe of the brain, when damaged, classically produces personality changes and impaired executive function/judgment?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The prefrontal cortex is central to executive function, judgment, and personality; its damage causes disinhibition, poor judgment, and personality change, as classically illustrated by the Phineas Gage case.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Damage to the non-dominant parietal lobe classically results in which clinical syndrome?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Non-dominant (usually right) parietal lobe lesions classically cause contralateral hemispatial neglect, where the patient ignores stimuli on the affected side.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The pineal gland, part of the epithalamus, primarily secretes which hormone regulating circadian rhythm?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The pineal gland secretes melatonin, which regulates circadian sleep-wake rhythms in response to light-dark cycles.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which structure connects the cerebellum to the brainstem, carrying afferent and efferent fibers?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The three pairs of cerebellar peduncles (superior, middle, inferior) connect the cerebellum to the midbrain, pons, and medulla respectively.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which of the following best describes decorticate posturing seen in severe brain injury?
o: Arm flexion with leg extension, indicating a lesion above the level of the red nucleus
Arm extension and leg extension, indicating a lower brainstem lesion
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Decorticate posturing (arm flexion, leg extension) suggests a lesion above the red nucleus (in the cerebral hemispheres or diencephalon), less severe than decerebrate posturing.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Decerebrate posturing, with extension of both arms and legs, suggests a lesion at which level?
o: At or below the level of the red nucleus (midbrain/brainstem)
Above the level of the red nucleus
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Decerebrate posturing (extension of all limbs) indicates a more caudal, brainstem-level lesion at or below the red nucleus, generally a worse prognostic sign than decorticate posturing.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The subthalamic nucleus, part of the basal ganglia circuitry, when damaged classically produces which movement disorder?
o: Hemiballismus (violent flinging movements of a limb)
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Lesions of the subthalamic nucleus classically produce hemiballismus, characterized by violent, involuntary flinging movements of the contralateral limb.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The spinal cord in adults typically terminates at which vertebral level?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The adult spinal cord terminates as the conus medullaris at approximately L1-L2.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway carries which sensory modalities?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The dorsal columns carry fine touch, vibration sense, and conscious proprioception, crossing in the medulla (medial lemniscus).

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The spinothalamic tract carries which sensory modalities and crosses at which level?
o: Pain and temperature; crosses within 1-2 spinal segments of entry
Vibration sense; crosses in the pons
Fine touch; crosses in the medulla
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature sensation, with fibers crossing near their level of entry into the spinal cord.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: A lesion causing loss of pain and temperature sensation on one side of the body but preserved proprioception, with contralateral motor weakness, describes which classic spinal cord syndrome?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Brown-Sequard syndrome (spinal cord hemisection) causes ipsilateral loss of motor function and proprioception/vibration, with contralateral loss of pain/temperature below the lesion.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Anterior cord syndrome, often due to anterior spinal artery occlusion, classically spares which sensory modality?
o: All sensory modalities are lost equally
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Anterior spinal artery occlusion affects the anterior two-thirds of the cord (corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts), sparing the dorsal columns supplied by the posterior spinal arteries.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which spinal tract is responsible for carrying descending voluntary motor commands from the cerebral cortex?
o: Rubrospinal tract as the primary pathway in humans
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The lateral corticospinal tract is the principal pathway for voluntary motor control in humans, carrying fibers from the motor cortex.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The dorsal root of a spinal nerve carries which type of fibers?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The dorsal (posterior) root carries sensory afferent fibers into the spinal cord, with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The ventral root of a spinal nerve carries which type of fibers?
o: Motor efferents (and preganglionic autonomic fibers at relevant levels)
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The ventral (anterior) root carries motor efferent fibers, and at thoracolumbar/sacral levels, preganglionic autonomic fibers.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The brachial plexus is formed by the ventral rami of which spinal nerve roots?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The brachial plexus arises from the ventral rami of C5 through T1.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The lumbar plexus is formed by the ventral rami of which spinal nerve roots?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The lumbar plexus is formed from the ventral rami of L1 through L4.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The sacral plexus, giving rise to the sciatic nerve, is formed by which nerve roots?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The sacral plexus arises from L4 through S4 ventral rami, giving rise to the sciatic nerve among other branches.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Damage to the radial nerve at the spiral groove of the humerus classically causes which deficit?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Radial nerve injury impairs wrist and finger extensors, causing wrist drop.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Damage to the ulnar nerve at the elbow (medial epicondyle) classically causes which deformity, especially with chronic injury?
o: Claw hand (ulnar claw), affecting the 4th and 5th digits most
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Ulnar nerve injury weakens the intrinsic hand muscles, causing hyperextension at the MCP joints and flexion at the IP joints of the 4th and 5th digits (ulnar claw).

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Median nerve injury at the wrist, as in carpal tunnel syndrome, classically causes sensory loss over which area?
o: Palmar aspect of the lateral 3.5 digits
Palmar aspect of the medial 1.5 digits
Dorsal aspect of the hand entirely
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The median nerve supplies sensation to the palmar surface of the thumb, index, middle, and half of the ring finger.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Erb's palsy, resulting from injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5-C6), classically produces which posture, often called the 'waiter's tip' position?
o: Arm adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Erb's palsy causes the characteristic 'waiter's tip' posture: shoulder adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated, wrist flexed.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Klumpke's palsy, resulting from injury to the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1), classically affects which hand function?
o: Intrinsic hand muscles, causing a claw hand deformity
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Klumpke's palsy affects the lower trunk (C8-T1), impairing intrinsic hand muscles and causing a claw hand, often with an associated Horner's syndrome.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Common fibular (peroneal) nerve injury at the fibular neck classically causes which deficit?
o: Foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Common fibular nerve injury impairs dorsiflexors and evertors of the foot, causing foot drop and a characteristic steppage gait.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The tibial nerve, the other terminal branch of the sciatic nerve, primarily supplies which muscle group and its injury causes what deficit?
o: Anterior compartment of the leg; causes foot drop
Quadriceps; causes loss of knee extension
Lateral compartment of the leg; causes loss of eversion only
Posterior compartment of the leg; injury impairs plantarflexion and toe flexion
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The tibial nerve innervates the posterior leg compartment (plantarflexors and toe flexors); injury impairs plantarflexion and toe flexion.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The femoral nerve, arising from the lumbar plexus, primarily innervates which muscle group?
o: Quadriceps femoris (knee extensors) and iliopsoas (hip flexor)
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The femoral nerve innervates the quadriceps (knee extension) and iliopsoas (hip flexion), and provides sensation to the anterior thigh and medial leg (via saphenous nerve).

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Injury to the long thoracic nerve, supplying serratus anterior, classically causes which clinical sign?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Long thoracic nerve injury weakens serratus anterior, causing a winged scapula, especially notable when pushing against a wall.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The dermatome supplying sensation to the nipple line corresponds to which spinal level?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The T4 dermatome corresponds to the nipple line, a useful clinical landmark for assessing sensory levels.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The dermatome supplying sensation to the umbilicus corresponds to which spinal level?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The T10 dermatome corresponds to the level of the umbilicus, another key clinical landmark.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which reflex tests the integrity of spinal levels L3-L4, commonly assessed clinically?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The patellar (knee jerk) reflex tests the integrity of the L3-L4 spinal segments via the femoral nerve.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The ankle jerk (Achilles) reflex tests the integrity of which spinal level(s)?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The ankle jerk reflex primarily tests S1-S2 spinal segments via the tibial nerve.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: A positive Babinski sign (extensor plantar response) in an adult indicates which type of lesion?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: An extensor plantar response (Babinski sign) in an adult indicates upper motor neuron pathology affecting the corticospinal tract.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Cauda equina syndrome results from compression of which structure, typically presenting with saddle anesthesia and bowel/bladder dysfunction?
o: The nerve roots below the conus medullaris (cauda equina)
The spinal cord itself above L1
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Cauda equina syndrome results from compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris, causing saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder dysfunction, and lower limb weakness.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The autonomic nervous system's sympathetic preganglionic neurons originate from which spinal cord region?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons arise from the intermediolateral cell column of the thoracolumbar (T1-L2) spinal cord.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Parasympathetic preganglionic neurons of the spinal cord arise from which segments, contributing to pelvic organ innervation?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Sacral parasympathetic outflow arises from S2-S4, forming the pelvic splanchnic nerves supplying pelvic viscera.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The dorsal root ganglion contains the cell bodies of which type of neurons?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The dorsal root ganglion houses pseudounipolar sensory neuron cell bodies, whose peripheral processes carry sensory information centrally.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which spinal cord region shows the greatest cross-sectional area of gray matter, corresponding to the innervation of the upper limb?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The cervical enlargement (C5-T1) contains increased gray matter to accommodate the dense innervation required for the upper limb.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The lumbar enlargement of the spinal cord corresponds to which spinal levels and serves which function?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The lumbar enlargement (approximately L2-S3 cord segments) provides the dense innervation required for the lower limb.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which structure anchors the spinal cord to the coccyx, an important landmark in understanding the conus medullaris' fixed position?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The filum terminale, a fibrous extension of the pia mater, anchors the conus medullaris to the coccyx.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which spinal cord tract carries unconscious proprioceptive information to the cerebellum?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The dorsal and ventral spinocerebellar tracts carry unconscious proprioceptive information from muscles and joints to the cerebellum for coordination.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: A peripheral nerve injury classified as neurapraxia involves which type of pathological change?
o: Temporary conduction block without structural axonal disruption, typically full recovery
Complete transection of the axon and its supporting structures
Complete nerve destruction with no recovery potential
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Neurapraxia is the mildest form of nerve injury, involving a temporary conduction block (often from compression) with structurally intact axons and typically complete recovery.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Axonotmesis, a more severe peripheral nerve injury than neurapraxia, is characterized by which feature?
o: Axonal disruption with preservation of the surrounding connective tissue sheaths (endoneurium intact), allowing regeneration
Complete transection of the entire nerve including connective tissue
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Axonotmesis involves axonal disruption with preserved connective tissue sheaths, allowing for regeneration and functional recovery over time, generally slower than neurapraxia recovery.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which nerve, arising from the sacral plexus, is the largest nerve in the human body?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The sciatic nerve, formed from L4-S3 roots, is the largest and widest single nerve in the body.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The axillary nerve, a branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus, primarily innervates which muscle, and its injury (e.g., from shoulder dislocation) causes what deficit?
o: Biceps brachii; loss of elbow flexion
Latissimus dorsi; loss of arm adduction
Supraspinatus; loss of shoulder abduction initiation
Deltoid; loss of shoulder abduction beyond the first 15 degrees and sensory loss over the 'regimental badge' area
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The axillary nerve innervates the deltoid and teres minor; injury (common with shoulder dislocation or surgical neck of humerus fracture) impairs abduction and causes sensory loss over the lateral shoulder.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: The obturator nerve, from the lumbar plexus, primarily innervates which muscle group and its injury impairs which movement?
o: Adductor muscles of the thigh; hip adduction
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: The obturator nerve innervates the medial (adductor) compartment of the thigh, and its injury impairs hip adduction.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which spinal nerve root is most commonly compressed in a posterolateral L4-L5 disc herniation?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: A posterolateral herniation at the L4-L5 level typically compresses the traversing L5 nerve root, which exits at the level below.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.s: Which of the following spinal cord syndromes results from a central cord lesion, classically seen after hyperextension injury in an elderly patient with pre-existing cervical spondylosis?
o: Pure sensory loss with normal motor function
Disproportionately greater weakness in the upper limbs compared to the lower limbs
Complete bilateral paralysis with no sparing
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.e: Central cord syndrome classically causes disproportionate upper limb weakness compared to lower limb weakness, due to the more central location of cervical and upper limb fibers within the corticospinal tract.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: The resting membrane potential of a typical neuron is closest to which value?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: The typical neuronal resting membrane potential is approximately -70 mV, determined mainly by potassium's equilibrium potential and membrane permeability.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: The rapid depolarization phase of the neuronal action potential is primarily due to which ionic event?
o: Rapid sodium influx through voltage-gated sodium channels
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Depolarization results from rapid opening of voltage-gated sodium channels, allowing sodium influx down its electrochemical gradient.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Repolarization of the neuronal action potential occurs primarily due to which ionic event?
o: Sodium channel inactivation and potassium efflux through voltage-gated potassium channels
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Repolarization results from inactivation of sodium channels and delayed opening of voltage-gated potassium channels, allowing potassium efflux.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: The absolute refractory period of a neuron corresponds to which physiological state?
o: A period during which only a very strong stimulus can elicit another action potential
The resting state prior to any stimulation
A period with no relevance to action potential generation
A period during which no stimulus, however strong, can elicit another action potential
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: During the absolute refractory period, sodium channels are inactivated, making it impossible to generate another action potential regardless of stimulus strength.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which type of synapse uses direct electrical continuity via gap junctions, allowing extremely fast signal transmission?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Electrical synapses use gap junctions for direct ionic current flow between cells, enabling very rapid, often bidirectional signal transmission.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: At a typical chemical synapse, arrival of an action potential at the presynaptic terminal triggers influx of which ion, leading to neurotransmitter release?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Calcium influx through voltage-gated calcium channels at the presynaptic terminal triggers synaptic vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which neurotransmitter is the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter throughout the CNS, acting on NMDA, AMPA, and kainate receptors.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which neurotransmitter is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain, acting via GABA-A (chloride channel) and GABA-B (G-protein coupled) receptors.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Glycine functions as the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in which part of the central nervous system?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Glycine is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord, acting on glycine receptors (chloride channels).

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Temporal summation at a postsynaptic neuron refers to which phenomenon?
o: Summation of successive postsynaptic potentials from a single presynaptic input firing in rapid succession
An action potential occurring without any stimulus
A decrease in synaptic strength over time
Summation of postsynaptic potentials from multiple presynaptic inputs arriving simultaneously at different locations
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Temporal summation occurs when successive postsynaptic potentials from repeated firing of a single input summate due to close timing, before decaying.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Spatial summation at a postsynaptic neuron refers to which phenomenon?
o: A form of long-term potentiation exclusively
Summation of potentials from a single input over time
An artifact with no physiological relevance
Summation of postsynaptic potentials from multiple different presynaptic inputs occurring simultaneously
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Spatial summation involves simultaneous input from multiple presynaptic neurons summating at the postsynaptic membrane to potentially reach threshold.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: The stretch (myotatic) reflex, such as the knee jerk reflex, is an example of which type of neural circuit?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: The stretch reflex is a classic monosynaptic reflex, with a direct synapse between the afferent sensory neuron (from muscle spindle) and the efferent motor neuron.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Muscle spindles, the sensory receptors for the stretch reflex, primarily detect which stimulus?
o: Muscle length and rate of change of length (stretch)
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Muscle spindles detect changes in muscle length and the velocity of stretch, providing proprioceptive feedback for reflex and voluntary motor control.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Golgi tendon organs, located at the muscle-tendon junction, primarily detect which stimulus and mediate which reflex?
o: Muscle tension; mediate the inverse myotatic (autogenic inhibition) reflex
Muscle length; mediate the stretch reflex
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Golgi tendon organs sense muscle tension and mediate the inverse myotatic reflex (autogenic inhibition), protecting muscles from excessive tension by inhibiting the agonist and exciting the antagonist.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: The withdrawal (flexor) reflex, in response to a painful stimulus, is an example of which type of reflex circuit?
o: Polysynaptic reflex involving multiple interneurons and often crossed extension
A reflex mediated solely by the cerebellum
A purely spinal reflex without interneurons
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: The withdrawal reflex is polysynaptic, involving interneurons that coordinate flexor withdrawal on the stimulated side and often crossed extension on the opposite side for balance.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which type of nerve fiber, according to the Erlanger-Gasser classification, has the largest diameter and fastest conduction velocity, associated with proprioception and motor function?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: A-alpha fibers are the largest, most heavily myelinated fibers with the fastest conduction velocity, associated with proprioception and skeletal motor function.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Type C nerve fibers, unmyelinated and with the slowest conduction velocity, are primarily associated with which sensory modality?
o: Slow, dull, aching pain and temperature
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Unmyelinated type C fibers conduct slowly and carry dull, aching, poorly localized pain and temperature sensation.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Saltatory conduction, occurring in myelinated axons, refers to which physiological process?
o: Conduction that occurs only in unmyelinated fibers
Action potentials 'jumping' between successive nodes of Ranvier, increasing conduction velocity
Slow continuous conduction along the entire axon membrane
A failure of action potential propagation
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: In myelinated axons, action potentials regenerate only at the nodes of Ranvier, effectively 'jumping' between nodes, greatly increasing conduction velocity.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Long-term potentiation (LTP), a cellular mechanism underlying learning and memory, is most closely associated with which brain structure?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: LTP, a persistent strengthening of synapses based on recent activity patterns, is extensively studied in the hippocampus and is considered a key mechanism of memory formation.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which receptor type is critical for the induction of long-term potentiation in the hippocampus, due to its voltage- and ligand-gated properties?
o: NMDA receptor (requiring both glutamate binding and depolarization to relieve magnesium block)
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: NMDA receptors require both glutamate binding and sufficient postsynaptic depolarization (to expel the magnesium block), making them coincidence detectors critical for LTP induction.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which of the following best describes the function of astrocytes in the central nervous system?
o: Metabolic support, blood-brain barrier maintenance, and regulation of extracellular ion/neurotransmitter concentration
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Astrocytes provide metabolic support to neurons, help form and maintain the blood-brain barrier, and regulate extracellular potassium and neurotransmitter levels.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which glial cell type is responsible for myelination of axons in the central nervous system?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Oligodendrocytes myelinate multiple CNS axons, in contrast to Schwann cells which myelinate a single segment of a peripheral axon each.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Microglia in the central nervous system primarily function as which cell type?
o: Resident immune cells/macrophages of the CNS
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Microglia are the resident macrophage-like immune cells of the CNS, involved in surveillance, phagocytosis, and inflammatory responses.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which type of receptor potential occurs in sensory receptors and is graded (proportional to stimulus intensity) rather than all-or-none?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Generator (receptor) potentials in sensory receptors are graded responses to stimulus intensity, which if sufficient, trigger action potentials in the associated afferent neuron.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which phenomenon describes the decrease in receptor response to a sustained, unchanging stimulus over time?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Sensory adaptation is the decline in receptor firing rate in response to a constant, unchanging stimulus over time.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Rapidly adapting (phasic) receptors, such as Pacinian corpuscles, are best suited to detect which type of stimulus?
o: Changes in stimulus, such as vibration or onset/offset of pressure
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Rapidly adapting receptors like Pacinian corpuscles respond best to changing stimuli (vibration, movement) rather than constant pressure.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Slowly adapting (tonic) receptors, such as Merkel discs, are best suited to detect which type of stimulus?
o: Sustained pressure or touch, providing continuous information about stimulus presence
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Slowly adapting receptors like Merkel discs continue firing throughout a sustained stimulus, providing ongoing information about static touch/pressure.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: The neuromuscular junction utilizes which neurotransmitter to trigger skeletal muscle contraction?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Acetylcholine released from motor neuron terminals acts on nicotinic receptors on the muscle end-plate, triggering depolarization and contraction.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which disease results from autoantibodies against the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction, causing fatigable muscle weakness?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Myasthenia gravis results from autoimmune destruction/blockade of postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, causing progressive muscle fatigue with repeated use.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which disease results from autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, impairing acetylcholine release, often paraneoplastic in origin?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome involves autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, impairing acetylcholine release, often associated with small cell lung cancer.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which of the following best describes the size principle of motor unit recruitment during voluntary muscle contraction?
o: Only the largest motor units are ever recruited
Larger motor units are recruited before smaller ones
Smaller (lower threshold) motor units are recruited before larger ones as force demand increases
Motor units are recruited randomly regardless of size
Recruitment order is unrelated to motor unit size
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: The size principle states that motor units are recruited in order from smallest (lowest threshold, fatigue-resistant) to largest as increasing force is required.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which type of skeletal muscle fiber is most resistant to fatigue, relying primarily on oxidative metabolism?
o: Type IIa only, not Type I
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Type I (slow oxidative/slow twitch) fibers are highly fatigue-resistant due to abundant mitochondria and reliance on oxidative metabolism.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which of the following best describes the physiological basis of referred pain, such as cardiac pain felt in the left arm?
o: Direct nerve damage to the arm
Convergence of visceral and somatic afferent fibers onto the same spinal cord neurons, causing the brain to misattribute the source
Random neural activity with no anatomical basis
Direct connection between the heart and the arm's peripheral nerves
Psychological factors only, with no physiological basis
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Referred pain results from convergence of visceral and somatic sensory afferents onto shared spinal neurons, so the brain, more accustomed to somatic input, misattributes visceral pain to a somatic dermatomal location.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which of the following neurotransmitters, acting on descending pain pathways from the periaqueductal gray, is involved in endogenous pain modulation and analgesia?
o: Serotonin and norepinephrine (via descending inhibitory pathways)
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Descending pain modulatory pathways from the periaqueductal gray, via the rostral ventromedial medulla, use serotonin and norepinephrine to inhibit ascending pain transmission at the spinal cord level.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: The gate control theory of pain proposes that activation of which type of afferent fiber can inhibit pain transmission at the spinal cord level?
o: Large-diameter A-beta fibers (touch/pressure), which can inhibit dorsal horn pain transmission neurons
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: The gate control theory suggests that activity in large-diameter A-beta touch fibers can inhibit dorsal horn transmission of pain signals from smaller nociceptive fibers, providing a physiological basis for treatments like rubbing an injured area.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which equation describes the relationship between the equilibrium potential of an ion and its concentration gradient across a membrane?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: The Nernst equation calculates the equilibrium potential for a specific ion based on its intracellular and extracellular concentrations.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: The Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation, unlike the Nernst equation, accounts for which additional factor in determining membrane potential?
o: The relative permeability of the membrane to multiple different ions simultaneously
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: The GHK equation calculates membrane potential considering the relative permeabilities and concentration gradients of multiple ions (Na+, K+, Cl-), unlike the single-ion Nernst equation.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which phase of the compound action potential recording corresponds to a period of decreased excitability immediately following an action potential, requiring a stronger-than-normal stimulus?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: The relative refractory period follows the absolute refractory period, during which a stronger-than-normal stimulus can still trigger another action potential, as some sodium channels have recovered from inactivation.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which of the following best describes 'presynaptic inhibition,' a mechanism for selectively reducing neurotransmitter release from a specific presynaptic terminal?
o: An effect that only occurs at the neuromuscular junction
A synapse acting on the axon terminal of another neuron (axo-axonic synapse) to reduce calcium influx and neurotransmitter release
Complete blockade of all synaptic transmission in the circuit
Direct inhibition of the postsynaptic membrane only
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Presynaptic inhibition typically involves an axo-axonic synapse that reduces calcium influx (or otherwise limits release machinery) at the target presynaptic terminal, selectively dampening its neurotransmitter output.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.s: Which of the following best explains why local anesthetics preferentially block smaller, unmyelinated pain fibers before larger, myelinated motor fibers at a given concentration?
o: Smaller fibers have a larger surface area to volume ratio and lack myelin, making them more susceptible to sodium channel blockade at lower concentrations
Local anesthetics only affect unmyelinated fibers
Larger fibers are blocked first in all cases
Motor fibers lack sodium channels entirely
Fiber size has no bearing on anesthetic sensitivity
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.e: Smaller, unmyelinated fibers are generally more sensitive to local anesthetic blockade at a given concentration due to their higher surface-area-to-volume ratio and lack of myelin, though clinical blockade patterns can be complex.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: The central nervous system develops embryologically from which germ layer?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: The CNS arises from the neuroectoderm, specifically via formation of the neural plate and subsequent neural tube.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: The neural tube forms through which embryological process?
o: Neurulation, involving folding and fusion of the neural plate
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Neurulation involves folding of the neural plate to form neural folds, which fuse dorsally to create the neural tube.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Failure of the neural tube to close at the cranial end results in which severe congenital anomaly?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Failure of cranial neuropore closure results in anencephaly, a severe and usually fatal defect involving absence of major brain structures.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Failure of the caudal neuropore to close results in which spectrum of congenital anomalies?
o: Spina bifida (ranging from occulta to myelomeningocele)
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Failure of caudal neuropore closure results in the spina bifida spectrum, from mild (occulta) to severe (myelomeningocele) forms.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: The three primary brain vesicles that form early in neural tube development are the prosencephalon, mesencephalon, and which third vesicle?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: The three primary vesicles are the prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain), and rhombencephalon (hindbrain).

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: The prosencephalon (forebrain) further subdivides into which two secondary vesicles?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: The prosencephalon divides into the telencephalon (cerebral hemispheres) and diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus, etc.).

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: The rhombencephalon (hindbrain) further subdivides into which two secondary vesicles?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: The rhombencephalon divides into the metencephalon (giving rise to the pons and cerebellum) and myelencephalon (giving rise to the medulla oblongata).

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Neural crest cells, arising from the margins of the neural plate, give rise to which of the following structures?
o: Peripheral nervous system ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla, and melanocytes, among others
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Neural crest cells are a remarkably versatile embryonic population, giving rise to peripheral neurons and glia, adrenal medullary cells, melanocytes, and craniofacial structures.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which congenital anomaly results from failure of the forebrain to properly divide into two cerebral hemispheres?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Holoprosencephaly results from incomplete cleavage of the forebrain into two hemispheres, often associated with midline facial defects.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Lissencephaly, a disorder of neuronal migration resulting in a smooth brain surface lacking normal gyri, results from abnormal function of which process?
o: Neuronal migration along radial glial fibers during cortical development
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Lissencephaly results from defective neuronal migration during cortical development, producing an abnormally smooth cerebral surface.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which histological cell is the principal functional signaling unit of nervous tissue, characterized by dendrites, a cell body, and an axon?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: The neuron is the fundamental structural and functional signaling unit of the nervous system.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Nissl bodies (substance), seen histologically in neuronal cell bodies, correspond to which organelle?
o: Rough endoplasmic reticulum and free ribosomes
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Nissl bodies represent clusters of rough endoplasmic reticulum and free ribosomes, reflecting the high protein synthetic activity of neurons.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which type of neuron, characterized by a single process that bifurcates, is typical of dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons are pseudounipolar, with a single process that bifurcates into peripheral and central branches.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Multipolar neurons, having multiple dendrites and a single axon, are the most common neuronal type and are typified by which cell?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Anterior horn motor neurons are classic examples of multipolar neurons, the most common morphological type in the CNS.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Bipolar neurons, with one dendrite and one axon, are typically found in which sensory system(s)?
o: Retina, olfactory epithelium, and vestibulocochlear ganglia
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Bipolar neurons are specialized sensory neurons found in the retina (bipolar cells), olfactory epithelium, and vestibulocochlear (auditory/vestibular) ganglia.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which histological structure, formed by myelin-producing Schwann cells wrapping around peripheral axons, contains gaps called nodes of Ranvier?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: The myelin sheath, formed by Schwann cells (PNS) or oligodendrocytes (CNS), is interrupted at regular intervals by nodes of Ranvier, enabling saltatory conduction.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which glial cell type lines the ventricles of the brain and central canal of the spinal cord, contributing to CSF circulation?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Ependymal cells form a ciliated epithelial lining of the ventricular system and central canal, aiding CSF flow and, in the choroid plexus, its production.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Purkinje cells, large neurons with extensively branching dendritic trees, are characteristically found in which brain structure?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Purkinje cells are the principal output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, characterized by their elaborate dendritic arborization and exclusively inhibitory (GABAergic) output.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which cell layer of the cerebral cortex is the primary source of output to subcortical structures such as the spinal cord and brainstem?
o: Layer VI exclusively for all outputs
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Layer V of the cerebral cortex contains large pyramidal neurons (including Betz cells in the motor cortex) that project to subcortical targets like the spinal cord.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which cortical layer is the primary recipient of thalamocortical sensory input?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Layer IV is the main target of thalamic sensory afferents, particularly well developed in primary sensory cortical areas.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Wallerian degeneration, occurring in the distal segment of a transected axon, involves which sequence of events?
o: The distal axon segment degenerates, along with its myelin sheath, while Schwann cells/macrophages clear debris
No degeneration occurs in either segment
The proximal segment degenerates while the distal segment survives
Only the myelin degenerates, the axon remains intact
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Wallerian degeneration describes degeneration of the axon and myelin distal to a nerve injury, with subsequent clearance by Schwann cells and macrophages, preparing for potential regeneration.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which of the following best describes the process of axonal regeneration in the peripheral nervous system following axonotmesis?
o: Only motor axons can regenerate, never sensory axons
Axons can regenerate along preserved endoneurial tubes, guided by Schwann cells, at a rate of about 1mm/day
Regeneration is impossible in the PNS
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: In the PNS, preserved endoneurial tubes and Schwann cells support axonal regrowth, typically proceeding at approximately 1 mm per day.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which of the following statements about central nervous system axonal regeneration, compared to the peripheral nervous system, is correct?
o: CNS axons never degenerate after injury
CNS and PNS regeneration occur at identical rates and with identical success
CNS regeneration requires no glial involvement at all
CNS regeneration is generally more robust than PNS regeneration
CNS regeneration is generally poor, partly due to inhibitory factors from oligodendrocytes and glial scarring
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: CNS regeneration is markedly limited compared to the PNS, due to factors including myelin-associated inhibitory proteins and glial scar formation by reactive astrocytes.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: The neural crest gives rise to the adrenal medulla, which is functionally analogous to which other neural crest derivative?
o: Postganglionic sympathetic neurons (chromaffin cells act as modified sympathetic neurons)
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Adrenal medullary chromaffin cells are functionally analogous to postganglionic sympathetic neurons, both being neural crest derivatives releasing catecholamines.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which of the following congenital anomalies of the cerebellum, involving cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum, is often associated with syringomyelia?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Arnold-Chiari malformation involves downward displacement of cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum, often associated with syringomyelia and hydrocephalus.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Dandy-Walker malformation is characterized by which key anatomical feature?
o: Cerebellar vermis agenesis/hypoplasia with cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle
Absence of the corpus callosum only
Neural tube closure defect at the cranial end
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Dandy-Walker malformation involves hypoplasia or agenesis of the cerebellar vermis with cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle, often with hydrocephalus.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which of the following best describes the histological hallmark of a demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis, when examined microscopically?
o: Plaques of demyelination with relative axonal preservation, particularly in white matter
Loss of neuronal cell bodies with preserved myelin
Formation of new neurons in affected areas
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Multiple sclerosis classically shows demyelinated plaques within CNS white matter, with variable axonal preservation, especially early in the disease.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which of the following cells provides myelination for a single internode of a single peripheral axon, in contrast to central myelinating cells that myelinate multiple axons?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Each Schwann cell myelinates only one internodal segment of a single peripheral axon, unlike oligodendrocytes which myelinate multiple CNS axons simultaneously.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Synaptic pruning, an important process in neural development, primarily refers to which phenomenon?
o: Formation of entirely new neurons in adulthood
Elimination of excess synaptic connections formed during early development, refining neural circuits
Formation of new blood vessels in the brain
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Synaptic pruning eliminates excess or unused synapses formed during early brain development, refining and optimizing neural circuitry based on activity and experience.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: The neural crest arises from which specific region of the developing neural tube?
o: The roof plate exclusively after tube closure
The margins (crests) of the neural folds, at the junction of neural and surface ectoderm
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Neural crest cells originate at the margins of the neural folds and undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition to migrate throughout the embryo.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which embryonic structure induces formation of the overlying neural plate from ectoderm, via secretion of signaling molecules?
o: The notochord and underlying mesoderm (via neural induction)
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: The underlying notochord and paraxial mesoderm induce the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate, a process called primary neural induction.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which part of the developing neural tube gives rise to the retina, an extension of the central nervous system?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: The optic vesicle, an outgrowth of the diencephalon, invaginates to form the optic cup, giving rise to the retina, making it a true extension of the CNS.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which glial cell type provides scaffolding for neuronal migration during cortical development, later differentiating into astrocytes in many cases?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Radial glial cells span the developing cortex and serve as scaffolds along which newly formed neurons migrate to their appropriate cortical layers.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Cortical neurons migrate to form the six-layered neocortex in which characteristic pattern relative to birth order?
o: Inside-out, with earliest-born neurons forming the deepest layers and later neurons migrating past them to more superficial layers
Outside-in, with earliest-born neurons forming the most superficial layers
Random migration with no relationship to birth order
Migration proceeds strictly in a lateral-to-medial direction only
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Cortical development follows an 'inside-out' pattern, where early-generated neurons form the deepest cortical layers, while later-generated neurons migrate past them to form progressively more superficial layers.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which of the following histological stains is classically used to visualize Nissl substance in neuronal cell bodies?
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Nissl stains such as cresyl violet selectively stain the RNA-rich rough endoplasmic reticulum and ribosomes (Nissl substance) within neuronal cell bodies.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which of the following best describes the role of microglia in the healthy, uninjured central nervous system?
o: They have no function in the healthy brain
They continuously survey the CNS microenvironment, participating in synaptic pruning and immune surveillance
They form the blood-brain barrier alone
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Even in the healthy brain, microglia continuously survey their environment, contribute to synaptic pruning during development, and provide baseline immune surveillance.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which of the following is the embryological origin of the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis), distinguishing it from the anterior pituitary?
o: A downgrowth of neuroectoderm from the diencephalon (infundibulum)
Rathke's pouch (oral ectoderm), same as the anterior pituitary
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: The posterior pituitary develops as a downgrowth of neuroectoderm from the diencephalon (the infundibulum), unlike the anterior pituitary which arises from oral ectoderm (Rathke's pouch).

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which of the following describes the histological structure of a typical peripheral nerve fascicle, from innermost to outermost connective tissue layer?
o: All three layers are functionally and structurally identical
Endoneurium (around individual axons), perineurium (around fascicles), epineurium (around the whole nerve)
Endoneurium surrounds the whole nerve, epineurium surrounds individual axons
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: From innermost to outermost: endoneurium surrounds individual nerve fibers, perineurium bundles fibers into fascicles, and epineurium encloses the entire nerve.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which of the following best describes the histological appearance of a Negri body, a diagnostic finding in rabies infection?
o: A structure found only in glial cells
A cytoplasmic (intracytoplasmic) eosinophilic inclusion body found in infected neurons, particularly in the hippocampus
A finding specific to the neuromuscular junction
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: Negri bodies are cytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions found in neurons (classically Purkinje cells and hippocampal pyramidal neurons) infected with the rabies virus.

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.s: Which of the following best describes the process and general timeline by which myelination of central nervous system tracts proceeds during human development?
o: All CNS tracts are fully myelinated by birth
Myelination occurs randomly with no developmental pattern
Myelination proceeds in a generally caudal-to-cranial and continues postnatally into young adulthood, with certain tracts (e.g., corticospinal) myelinating relatively later
Myelination is completed entirely in utero
nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.e: CNS myelination follows a generally predictable sequence, beginning prenatally and continuing well into childhood and adolescence (and even into young adulthood for some association areas), with functionally more complex tracts myelinating later.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: The autonomic nervous system is divided into which two main efferent divisions?
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The two main efferent divisions of the autonomic nervous system are the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems, generally exerting opposing effects.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: The enteric nervous system, sometimes called the 'second brain,' is primarily responsible for regulating which system independently, though modulated by autonomic input?
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The enteric nervous system can independently regulate GI motility and secretion via its intrinsic neural networks (myenteric and submucosal plexuses), modulated by but not fully dependent on autonomic input.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons release which neurotransmitter at the synapse with postganglionic neurons?
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Both sympathetic and parasympathetic preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine, acting on nicotinic receptors of postganglionic neurons.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Most postganglionic sympathetic neurons release which neurotransmitter at their target organs?
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Most postganglionic sympathetic fibers release norepinephrine, acting on adrenergic receptors, with a notable exception being sweat glands (acetylcholine).

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Postganglionic parasympathetic neurons release which neurotransmitter at their target organs?
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Postganglionic parasympathetic neurons release acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors at their effector organs.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Stimulation of beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the heart produces which effect?
o: Increased heart rate and contractility (positive chronotropic and inotropic effects)
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Beta-1 adrenergic receptor stimulation in the heart increases heart rate (chronotropy) and contractility (inotropy).

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Stimulation of beta-2 adrenergic receptors in the bronchi produces which effect, relevant to asthma treatment?
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Beta-2 receptor stimulation relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, causing bronchodilation, the basis for beta-2 agonist use in asthma.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Stimulation of alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in blood vessels produces which effect?
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Alpha-1 receptor stimulation causes vascular smooth muscle contraction, resulting in vasoconstriction and increased peripheral resistance.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Muscarinic receptor stimulation at the heart, via the vagus nerve, produces which effect?
o: Increased conduction velocity through the AV node
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Vagal (parasympathetic) muscarinic stimulation of the heart, primarily via M2 receptors, decreases heart rate and slows AV nodal conduction.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which autonomic division is primarily responsible for the 'fight or flight' response?
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The sympathetic nervous system mediates the 'fight or flight' response, preparing the body for perceived threats through widespread physiological changes.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which autonomic division is primarily responsible for 'rest and digest' functions?
o: Enteric nervous system exclusively without other input
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The parasympathetic nervous system promotes 'rest and digest' activities, conserving energy and promoting digestion, when the body is not under acute threat.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Horner's syndrome, characterized by ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis, results from disruption of which pathway?
o: Somatic motor pathway to facial muscles
Sympathetic pathway to the head and neck (oculosympathetic pathway)
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Horner's syndrome results from interruption anywhere along the sympathetic (oculosympathetic) pathway supplying the eye and face, causing ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which cranial nerve carries parasympathetic fibers responsible for pupillary constriction (miosis) via the ciliary ganglion?
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: CN III carries parasympathetic fibers that synapse in the ciliary ganglion, innervating the sphincter pupillae muscle for pupillary constriction.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: The vagus nerve (CN X) provides parasympathetic innervation to which of the following organ systems?
o: Heart, lungs, and most of the gastrointestinal tract (to the splenic flexure)
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The vagus nerve provides extensive parasympathetic innervation to thoracic and abdominal viscera, including the heart, lungs, and GI tract up to the splenic flexure.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following best describes the sleep stage characterized by rapid eye movements, vivid dreaming, and low-voltage, high-frequency EEG activity resembling wakefulness?
o: No specific stage shows these features
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: REM sleep is characterized by rapid eye movements, vivid dreaming, muscle atonia, and EEG activity resembling wakefulness, despite being a distinct sleep state.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Slow-wave sleep (stage N3), characterized by high-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves on EEG, is thought to be important for which function?
o: Physical restoration and growth hormone release
Memory consolidation exclusively, with no other function
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Slow-wave (deep) sleep is associated with physical restoration processes and is the period of maximal growth hormone secretion.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus functions as which of the following?
o: The master circadian pacemaker, receiving direct retinal input
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The suprachiasmatic nucleus serves as the master biological clock, entrained by light input from the retina via the retinohypothalamic tract, regulating circadian rhythms.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which hypothalamic nucleus, when damaged, classically results in hyperphagia and obesity due to loss of satiety signaling?
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The ventromedial hypothalamic nucleus functions as a satiety center; its damage classically causes hyperphagia and subsequent obesity.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Damage to the lateral hypothalamic nucleus, sometimes called the hunger center, classically results in which effect?
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The lateral hypothalamus functions as a hunger/feeding center; its destruction classically causes aphagia (reduced feeding) and weight loss.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following brain structures is primarily responsible for the sensation of thirst, integrating osmotic and volume signals?
o: Hypothalamus (particularly circumventricular organs like the organum vasculosum)
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors, particularly within circumventricular organs lacking a full blood-brain barrier, sense plasma osmolarity and drive thirst.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following best describes the role of the prefrontal cortex in executive function?
o: It is solely responsible for basic reflexes
It functions independently of any connections with other brain regions
It is central to planning, decision-making, impulse control, and social behavior regulation
It exclusively processes primary sensory information
It has no role in decision-making or planning
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The prefrontal cortex integrates information for complex cognitive processes including planning, decision-making, impulse control, and social behavior regulation.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which type of memory, exemplified by riding a bicycle or typing, is classified as implicit (non-declarative) and often relies on the basal ganglia and cerebellum?
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Procedural memory, involving learned motor skills and habits, is a form of implicit memory that relies substantially on the basal ganglia and cerebellum, distinct from hippocampal-dependent declarative memory.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which type of memory refers to the conscious recollection of specific personal experiences and events, tied to a particular time and place?
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Episodic memory involves conscious recollection of specific personal events and experiences, contextualized in time and place, a subtype of declarative memory.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Semantic memory, another form of declarative memory, refers to which type of knowledge?
o: General factual knowledge about the world, independent of personal context
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Semantic memory encompasses general factual knowledge (facts, concepts, vocabulary) that is not tied to a specific personal experience or context.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following best describes the physiological basis of the pupillary light reflex, an autonomic reflex?
o: Purely a somatic reflex with no autonomic component
A reflex that does not involve the brainstem
Afferent via the optic nerve, efferent via parasympathetic fibers of the oculomotor nerve, causing pupillary constriction
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The pupillary light reflex has an afferent limb via the optic nerve (CN II) and an efferent parasympathetic limb via the oculomotor nerve (CN III), synapsing in the ciliary ganglion, causing pupillary constriction bilaterally (consensual reflex).

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which brainstem center, integrating input from higher cortical areas, hypothalamus, and chemoreceptors, is primarily responsible for generating the basic rhythm of breathing?
o: Medullary respiratory centers (dorsal and ventral respiratory groups)
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The medullary respiratory centers generate the basic automatic rhythm of breathing, modulated by pontine centers and higher cortical/chemoreceptor input.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following best describes the role of the cerebellum in motor learning, as distinct from its role in real-time movement coordination?
o: The cerebellum only stores memories, never adapts movement
Motor learning is purely a cortical phenomenon with no cerebellar involvement
Motor learning occurs exclusively in the basal ganglia
The cerebellum has no role in motor learning
The cerebellum contributes to adaptive motor learning by refining movements based on error feedback over repeated practice
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Beyond real-time coordination, the cerebellum plays a key role in motor learning, using error-based feedback (e.g., via climbing fiber input) to refine and adapt movements with practice.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following best describes the innervation and function of the adrenal medulla, distinguishing it from a typical sympathetic ganglion?
o: It receives postganglionic sympathetic fibers and releases norepinephrine into local tissue only
It has no autonomic innervation at all
It is innervated by somatic motor neurons
It receives preganglionic sympathetic fibers directly (via splanchnic nerves) and releases catecholamines (mainly epinephrine) directly into the bloodstream, acting as a modified sympathetic ganglion
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The adrenal medulla is directly innervated by preganglionic sympathetic fibers (via splanchnic nerves) and releases catecholamines, predominantly epinephrine, into the systemic circulation, functioning essentially as a specialized sympathetic ganglion.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which autonomic receptor subtype, when stimulated, mediates smooth muscle relaxation in the gut wall as part of parasympathetic-independent enteric control, alongside VIP and NO?
o: Nicotinic receptors on enteric neurons mediate fast synaptic transmission within enteric ganglia
Beta-2 receptors on smooth muscle have no role in the gut
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Nicotinic receptors mediate fast synaptic transmission between enteric neurons within the enteric ganglia, an important feature of the semi-autonomous enteric nervous system.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following autonomic changes would be expected during the parasympathetically-mediated phase of sexual response, specifically penile erection?
o: Parasympathetic-mediated vasodilation of penile arterioles (via nitric oxide release), causing erection
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Erection is primarily a parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic nerve) mediated event, with nitric oxide causing smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation of penile arterioles.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Ejaculation is primarily mediated by which autonomic division, in contrast to the parasympathetic control of erection?
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Emission and ejaculation are primarily mediated by sympathetic nervous system activation, contrasting with parasympathetic control of erection ('point and shoot' mnemonic: Parasympathetic for Point/erection, Sympathetic for Shoot/ejaculation).

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following best describes baroreceptor reflex control of blood pressure as an autonomic function integrated in the medulla?
o: Increased blood pressure always increases sympathetic outflow
Baroreceptors are located exclusively in the brain
Baroreceptor reflexes only affect respiratory rate
Baroreceptors have no connection to autonomic outflow
Increased blood pressure detected by carotid sinus/aortic arch baroreceptors leads to increased parasympathetic and decreased sympathetic outflow, lowering heart rate and blood pressure
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Rising blood pressure increases baroreceptor firing, which via the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla, increases parasympathetic (vagal) and decreases sympathetic outflow, reducing heart rate and vascular resistance to lower blood pressure.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following best describes the autonomic changes seen during acute stress response, beyond simple sympathetic activation, involving the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis?
o: Only sympathetic nervous system activation occurs, with no hormonal component
The HPA axis has no role in the stress response
Only parasympathetic activation occurs during stress
Hypothalamic CRH stimulates pituitary ACTH release, which stimulates adrenal cortisol secretion, complementing sympathetic-adrenal-medullary catecholamine release
Stress exclusively involves the enteric nervous system
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The stress response involves both rapid sympathetic-adrenal-medullary catecholamine release and the slower hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, with CRH-ACTH-cortisol providing sustained metabolic and immune modulatory effects.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following best describes the concept of 'homeostasis' as it relates to autonomic nervous system function?
o: A process that does not involve the nervous system
A process exclusive to the endocrine system
A fixed, unchanging internal state regardless of external conditions
A term relevant only to temperature regulation
The maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment through dynamic physiological regulation, heavily reliant on autonomic feedback mechanisms
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Homeostasis refers to the dynamic maintenance of a stable internal environment (temperature, blood pressure, pH, etc.), substantially mediated through autonomic nervous system feedback and effector mechanisms.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following statements about the effect of aging on autonomic nervous system function is most accurate?
o: Autonomic function is unaffected by aging
Aging is associated with reduced baroreceptor sensitivity and altered autonomic reflexes, contributing to conditions like orthostatic hypotension
Aging always increases parasympathetic tone exclusively
Autonomic aging effects are identical across all organ systems with no variability
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Aging is generally associated with reduced baroreceptor reflex sensitivity and altered autonomic responsiveness, contributing to a higher prevalence of orthostatic hypotension and other autonomic dysregulation in older adults.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following best describes 'autonomic dysreflexia,' a potentially life-threatening condition seen in patients with spinal cord injury above approximately T6?
o: A benign, asymptomatic finding with no clinical significance
A condition causing only mild, transient hypotension
A condition exclusively affecting the respiratory system
An exaggerated, unopposed sympathetic response to a noxious stimulus below the level of injury, causing severe hypertension, often with bradycardia due to intact vagal reflex above the lesion
A purely psychological phenomenon with no physiological basis
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Autonomic dysreflexia results from an exaggerated sympathetic reflex response to a stimulus (e.g., bladder distension) below a high spinal cord lesion, uninhibited by descending control, causing severe hypertension with compensatory bradycardia via the intact vagal reflex above the lesion; it is a medical emergency.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following best describes the neurophysiological concept of 'consciousness' in relation to the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS)?
o: Consciousness depends solely on the cerebellum
The ARAS has no role in sleep-wake regulation
Consciousness is entirely localized to a single cortical area with no brainstem contribution
The ARAS, projecting from the brainstem to the thalamus and cortex, is essential for maintaining arousal and wakefulness, a prerequisite for conscious awareness
Consciousness is purely a function of the spinal cord
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The ascending reticular activating system, through widespread projections from the brainstem to the thalamus and cortex, maintains cortical arousal and wakefulness, which is necessary (though perhaps not sufficient alone) for conscious awareness.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following best describes 'habituation,' a simple form of non-associative learning?
o: An increased response to a repeated, harmless stimulus over time
A form of associative learning requiring paired stimuli
A permanent, irreversible change in behavior
A process exclusive to invertebrate nervous systems
A decreased behavioral response to a repeated, harmless stimulus over time
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Habituation is a simple, non-associative form of learning in which the response to a repeated, non-threatening stimulus progressively decreases over time.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following best describes 'sensitization,' another simple form of non-associative learning, as contrasted with habituation?
o: A form of long-term memory exclusively
An enhanced response to a variety of stimuli following exposure to a strong or noxious stimulus
A process that only occurs in sensory neurons, never affecting motor output
Identical to habituation in mechanism and effect
A decreased response to any stimulus following a strong or noxious stimulus
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: Sensitization involves an enhanced behavioral response to a range of stimuli following exposure to a strong, noxious, or threatening stimulus, essentially the opposite effect of habituation.

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.s: Which of the following statements about the role of the cingulate gyrus, part of the limbic system, is most accurate?
o: It functions only in visual processing
It is exclusively a primary motor area
It has no involvement with emotion or pain processing
It participates in emotional processing, pain perception (particularly the affective/unpleasant component), and attention regulation
It is solely responsible for language production
nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.e: The cingulate gyrus, as part of the limbic system, is involved in emotional processing, the affective dimension of pain perception, and cognitive functions including attention and conflict monitoring.

special-senses/eye-anatomy-and-visual-pa.s: Which layer of the eyeball is the outermost fibrous layer, comprising the cornea and sclera?
special-senses/eye-anatomy-and-visual-pa.e: The fibrous tunic, the outermost layer, consists of the transparent cornea anteriorly and the opaque sclera posteriorly.

special-senses/eye-anatomy-and-visual-pa.s: The middle vascular layer of the eye, the uvea, consists of which three structures?
special-senses/eye-anatomy-and-visual-pa.e: The uvea (uveal tract) comprises the iris, ciliary body, and choroid, providing vascular supply and pigmentation.

special-senses/eye-anatomy-and-visual-pa.s: Aqueous humor is produced by which structure and drains via which pathway?
o: Produced by the retina; drains via the optic nerve
Produced by the lens; drains into the vitreous
Produced by the ciliary body; drains via the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal
Produced by the cornea; drains via the conjunctiva
Produced by the choroid; drains via the sclera
special-senses/eye-anatomy-and-visual-pa.e: The ciliary body's non-pigmented epithelium secretes aqueous humor, which drains primarily via the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal.

special-senses/eye-anatomy-and-visual-pa.s: Increased resistance to aqueous humor outflow, raising intraocular pressure, is the underlying mechanism of which common eye disease?
