special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.e: After sudden cessation of rotation, persistent cupula deflection (from ongoing endolymph inertia) continues to signal rotation to the brain, conflicting with visual and proprioceptive input indicating stillness, disrupting postural control and balance reflexes temporarily.

special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.s: Which of the following best describes the vestibulo-collic reflex, another vestibular-mediated postural reflex?
o: A reflex stabilizing head position in space by adjusting neck muscle activity in response to vestibular input
A purely voluntary neck movement mechanism
A reflex found only in the auditory system
A reflex that has no relationship to head position
A reflex controlling eye movement exclusively
special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.e: The vestibulo-collic reflex uses vestibular input to adjust neck muscle activity, helping stabilize head position and orientation in space during body movement.

special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.s: Which of the following best describes why patients with vestibular dysfunction often show improved balance with their eyes open compared to eyes closed?
o: Vision has no role in balance under any circumstances
Visual input can partially compensate for deficient vestibular information, helping maintain balance (a principle exploited in the Romberg test)
The Romberg test assesses hearing, not balance
Eyes open always worsens balance in vestibular disorders
special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.e: Visual input provides an additional sensory channel for spatial orientation that can partially compensate for deficient vestibular signals; the Romberg test exploits this by comparing balance with eyes open versus closed to help localize a balance disorder to the vestibular/proprioceptive system when balance worsens significantly with eye closure.

special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.s: Which of the following best describes the concept of 'vestibular habituation' exercises used in the rehabilitation of chronic dizziness?
o: Repeated exposure to provocative movements to promote central adaptation and reduce symptomatic responses over time
A surgical procedure to remove the vestibular organs
A one-time treatment providing permanent immediate cure
A medication that eliminates all vestibular function
An approach that worsens vestibular symptoms deliberately with no therapeutic goal
special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.e: Vestibular habituation exercises involve repeated, controlled exposure to symptom-provoking movements, promoting central nervous system adaptation and reduced symptomatic response over time, a cornerstone of vestibular rehabilitation therapy.

special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.s: Which of the following best explains the physiological basis of why very low-frequency sounds are harder for humans to localize precisely compared to mid-range frequencies?
o: Localization ability is identical across all frequencies
Low frequency sounds cannot be heard at all
The vestibular system, not the auditory system, localizes sound
Only high frequencies use interaural time differences

Interaural time difference cues become ambiguous at low frequencies because the wavelength becomes large relative to head size, while interaural intensity differences are minimal at low frequencies since sound diffracts around the head
special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.e: At low frequencies, interaural time difference cues become ambiguous due to phase ambiguity when wavelength exceeds head-related path differences, while interaural intensity differences are minimal because long wavelengths diffract easily around the head, together making precise localization of low-frequency sounds more difficult than for mid-range frequencies.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The eye develops embryologically as an outgrowth of which structure?
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The eye develops from an outgrowth of the diencephalon (optic vesicle), which induces overlying surface ectoderm to form the lens.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The lens of the eye develops embryologically from which tissue?
o: Surface ectoderm (lens placode, induced by the optic vesicle)
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The lens forms from surface ectoderm, induced by the underlying optic vesicle to form the lens placode, which invaginates to form the lens vesicle.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The retina develops from which part of the optic vesicle/optic cup?
o: Only the outer layer, forming the entire retina
The outer layer of the optic cup, forming the retinal pigment epithelium, and the inner layer, forming the neurosensory retina
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The optic cup's outer layer becomes the retinal pigment epithelium, while the inner layer differentiates into the multilayered neurosensory retina.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Coloboma, a congenital defect resulting in a gap or notch in ocular structures (iris, retina, choroid), results from failure of which embryological process?
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Coloboma results from incomplete closure of the choroid (optic) fissure during the fifth to seventh week of development, leaving a gap in affected ocular structures.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The corneal endothelium and stroma are derived embryologically from which tissue?
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Neural crest cells migrate to form the corneal endothelium and much of the corneal stroma, while surface ectoderm forms the corneal epithelium.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The inner ear (membranous labyrinth) develops embryologically from which structure?
o: Otic placode (surface ectoderm), invaginating to form the otic vesicle (otocyst)
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The inner ear membranous labyrinth develops from the otic placode, a thickening of surface ectoderm that invaginates to form the otic vesicle (otocyst).

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The middle ear cavity and Eustachian tube develop embryologically from which pharyngeal pouch derivative?
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The first pharyngeal pouch forms the tubotympanic recess, giving rise to the middle ear cavity and the Eustachian tube.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The malleus and incus, two of the three auditory ossicles, develop embryologically from which pharyngeal arch?
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The malleus and incus derive from first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage) mesenchyme, while the stapes derives mainly from the second arch (Reichert's cartilage).

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The external auditory canal develops embryologically from which structure?
o: Neural crest cells directly forming the canal
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The external auditory meatus develops from the first pharyngeal (branchial) cleft.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The auricle (pinna) develops from proliferations of mesenchyme surrounding which pharyngeal structure, called the hillocks of His?
o: The first and second pharyngeal arches
Neural crest cells with no arch contribution
The third and fourth pharyngeal arches only
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The auricle develops from six mesenchymal proliferations (hillocks of His) arising from the first and second pharyngeal arches surrounding the first pharyngeal cleft.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Congenital hearing loss can result from maternal infection during pregnancy with which classic teratogenic virus, alongside cardiac and ocular defects?
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Congenital rubella syndrome classically causes a triad of sensorineural hearing loss, cataracts, and cardiac defects (such as patent ductus arteriosus) when maternal infection occurs during early pregnancy.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Olfactory receptor neurons, responsible for the sense of smell, are unique among neurons in that they undergo which process throughout life?
o: They are replaced only once, in early childhood
Continuous regeneration/replacement from basal stem cells in the olfactory epithelium
They regenerate only in response to injury, never normally
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Olfactory receptor neurons are unusual in undergoing continuous turnover throughout life, regenerating from basal stem cells in the olfactory epithelium.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Olfactory receptor neuron axons pass through which structure to reach the olfactory bulb?
o: Cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Olfactory nerve fibers pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to synapse in the olfactory bulb.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Taste buds are located primarily on which structures of the tongue and oral cavity?
o: Fungiform, circumvallate, and foliate papillae (not filiform)
Uniformly on all tongue papillae including filiform
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Taste buds are found on fungiform, circumvallate, and foliate papillae, as well as the soft palate and epiglottis, but notably not on filiform papillae, which are purely mechanical/tactile.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The anterior two-thirds of the tongue receives taste sensation via which cranial nerve?
o: Facial nerve (CN VII), via the chorda tympani
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The posterior one-third of the tongue receives taste sensation via which cranial nerve?
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) carries taste sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Taste sensation from the epiglottis and pharynx is carried by which cranial nerve?
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The vagus nerve (CN X) carries taste sensation from the epiglottis and pharyngeal region.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which five basic taste modalities are classically recognized by the gustatory system?
o: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami
Sweet, bitter, hot, cold, and umami
Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and spicy
Sweet, salty, spicy, sour, and cold
Sweet, sour, bitter, metallic, and umami
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The five classically recognized basic tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami (savory, associated with glutamate).

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which type of taste receptor mechanism is used for sour taste transduction, related to hydrogen ion concentration?
o: Direct ion channel mechanisms sensitive to hydrogen ion concentration
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Sour taste transduction involves ion channels (including proton channels) directly sensitive to hydrogen ion concentration in acidic substances.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which taste modality relies on G-protein coupled receptors (T1R and T2R family receptors) for its transduction mechanism, notably including bitter taste?
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Sweet and umami tastes use T1R family GPCRs, while bitter taste uses the T2R family of GPCRs, in contrast to the more direct ion channel mechanisms of salty and sour taste.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Anosmia (loss of smell) is a recognized early symptom of which neurodegenerative disease, sometimes preceding motor symptoms by years?
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Anosmia is a well-recognized, often early, non-motor symptom of Parkinson's disease, sometimes preceding classic motor symptoms by years.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which of the following best describes the histological structure of the olfactory epithelium, distinguishing its receptor cells from typical epithelial cells?
o: A simple squamous epithelium with no specialized receptor cells
A pseudostratified columnar epithelium containing bipolar olfactory receptor neurons, supporting cells, and basal stem cells
Simple cuboidal epithelium without neuronal cells
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The olfactory epithelium is pseudostratified columnar, containing three main cell types: bipolar olfactory receptor neurons, supporting (sustentacular) cells, and basal stem cells for regeneration.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The ciliary body and iris develop embryologically from which two tissue sources?
o: Neuroectoderm (optic cup margin) and neural crest-derived mesenchyme
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The ciliary body and iris epithelium derive from the neuroectoderm of the optic cup margin, while their stroma and muscles derive largely from neural crest-derived mesenchyme.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The vitreous body of the eye develops from which embryological source, along with contribution from the hyaloid vascular system?
o: Mesenchyme (including neural crest and some surface ectoderm-associated contributions) surrounding the developing lens and optic cup, with early vascular contribution from the hyaloid system
Purely from the retinal pigment epithelium
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The vitreous body forms from mesenchymal tissue within the optic cup, with early contribution from the transient hyaloid vascular system, which normally regresses before birth.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which of the following congenital ocular anomalies results from persistence of the fetal hyaloid vascular system, potentially causing a retrolental mass and leukocoria?
o: Persistent fetal vasculature (previously called persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous)
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Persistent fetal vasculature results from failure of the hyaloid vascular system to regress normally, which can cause a retrolental mass, cataract, and leukocoria, and must be differentiated from retinoblastoma.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which of the following best describes the histological layers of the cornea, from anterior to posterior?
o: Stroma, epithelium, endothelium, Bowman's layer, Descemet's membrane (random order)
Only epithelium and stroma, with no basement membrane layers
Epithelium, Bowman's layer, stroma, Descemet's membrane, endothelium
A single uniform layer with no distinct sublayers
Endothelium, stroma, epithelium only, with no intervening layers
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The cornea has five classic histological layers from anterior to posterior: epithelium, Bowman's layer, stroma, Descemet's membrane, and endothelium.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which corneal layer is a single layer of cells responsible for maintaining corneal deturgescence (relative dehydration) via active ion pumping, and does not regenerate if significantly damaged?
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The corneal endothelium, a single layer of cells, actively pumps ions (and thus water) out of the stroma to maintain corneal transparency; unlike the epithelium, endothelial cells have very limited regenerative capacity in adults.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) performs which important function related to photoreceptor health?
o: Phagocytosis of shed photoreceptor outer segment discs and recycling of visual pigment components
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The RPE phagocytoses shed outer segment discs from photoreceptors and participates in recycling retinoid components of the visual cycle, essential for ongoing photoreceptor function and health.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which of the following histological layers of the retina contains the cell bodies of photoreceptors (rods and cones)?
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The outer nuclear layer of the retina contains the nuclei (cell bodies) of the rod and cone photoreceptors.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which retinal layer contains the cell bodies of retinal ganglion cells, whose axons form the nerve fiber layer and ultimately the optic nerve?
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The ganglion cell layer contains the cell bodies of retinal ganglion cells, whose axons collect in the nerve fiber layer before converging to form the optic nerve.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Muller cells, the principal glial cells of the retina, span nearly the entire retinal thickness and perform which function?
o: Formation of the vitreous body exclusively
Structural support and metabolic/homeostatic support for retinal neurons, analogous to astrocytes elsewhere in the CNS
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Muller cells span the retina radially, providing structural support and performing metabolic and homeostatic functions for retinal neurons, similar to the role astrocytes play elsewhere in the central nervous system.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which of the following describes the histological hallmark of glaucomatous optic nerve damage, visible on fundoscopic examination as disease progresses?
o: Progressive optic disc cupping (increased cup-to-disc ratio) due to loss of retinal ganglion cell axons
Retinal hemorrhages exclusively without disc changes
Optic disc pallor without any cupping
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Glaucoma classically causes progressive optic disc cupping, reflecting loss of retinal ganglion cell axons and supporting tissue, visible as an enlarging cup-to-disc ratio on fundoscopic examination.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: The sclera, the tough outer coat of the posterior eye, is composed primarily of which tissue type?
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The sclera is composed of dense, irregularly arranged collagenous connective tissue, providing structural rigidity and protection to the eyeball.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which of the following best describes the structure and function of the tectorial membrane within the organ of Corti?
o: A structure with no functional role in hearing
A membrane found only in the vestibular system, not the cochlea
A bony structure providing rigid support
The membrane separating the scala vestibuli from the scala media
A gelatinous membrane overlying the hair cells, whose relative movement against the stereocilia during basilar membrane vibration causes stereocilia deflection and hair cell stimulation
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The tectorial membrane overlies the hair cells of the organ of Corti; relative shearing motion between it and the basilar membrane during sound-induced vibration deflects the stereocilia, triggering mechanotransduction.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which of the following best describes the histological structure of the stria vascularis within the cochlea, and its physiological importance?
o: A vascularized epithelium lining the scala media that generates the endocochlear potential and maintains the ionic composition of endolymph
A remnant of embryological development with no adult function
An avascular structure with no metabolic role
A structure found only in the vestibular apparatus
The site of sound wave reception from the middle ear
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The stria vascularis, a highly vascularized epithelium lining the scala media, actively generates the endocochlear potential and maintains the unique high-potassium ionic composition of endolymph, essential for normal hair cell function.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which of the following best describes the vestibular hair cell's arrangement of stereocilia and a single kinocilium, relevant to the direction-sensitive nature of vestibular transduction?
o: All stereocilia are of identical height with no polarity
Stereocilia are arranged randomly with no functional polarity

Stereocilia are arranged in rows of increasing height, with a single kinocilium at the tallest end, giving the hair cell directional sensitivity (deflection toward the kinocilium depolarizes, away hyperpolarizes)
The kinocilium is located at the shortest end of the stereocilia bundle
There is no kinocilium in vestibular hair cells
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Vestibular hair cells have stereocilia arranged in a graded height pattern with a single kinocilium at the tallest edge; deflection toward the kinocilium depolarizes the cell, while deflection away hyperpolarizes it, providing inherent directional sensitivity.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which of the following best describes the embryological origin of the extraocular muscles, distinguishing them from most other skeletal muscles derived from somites?
o: They have no distinct embryological origin from other skeletal muscle
They arise entirely from neural crest cells
They arise from prechordal mesoderm and cranial paraxial mesoderm (preotic somitomeres), not from typical somites
They arise from lateral plate mesoderm exclusively, like limb muscles
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Extraocular muscles arise from prechordal plate mesoderm and cranial paraxial mesoderm (preotic somitomeres), a distinct origin from the somite-derived skeletal muscles of the trunk and limbs, which explains their unique molecular and immunological properties.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which of the following best describes the embryological development of the eyelids, including the transient period during which they are fused?
o: Eyelids form from surface ectoderm folds that fuse together transiently during the embryonic period and reopen before birth, typically by around the 26th to 28th week
Eyelids remain fused throughout gestation and open only after birth
Eyelids form from neural crest tissue exclusively without ectodermal contribution
Eyelid development is unrelated to surface ectoderm
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: The eyelids develop from surface ectodermal folds that grow toward each other and transiently fuse during development, typically reopening by around 26-28 weeks of gestation, allowing the eyes to be open at term.

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which of the following best describes microphthalmia, a congenital ocular anomaly?
o: A normal variant with no clinical significance
A defect limited only to the cornea
An abnormally small, underdeveloped eye, which can result from various insults during early ocular development including congenital infections
A condition exclusively affecting the eyelids
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Microphthalmia refers to an abnormally small and often malformed eye, which can result from disruptions in early ocular development due to genetic factors or environmental insults such as congenital infections (e.g., rubella, toxoplasmosis).

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.s: Which of the following best describes the role of neural crest cells in the development of the anterior segment of the eye, and the clinical relevance of their abnormal development?
o: Anterior segment structures are entirely derived from surface ectoderm with no mesenchymal contribution
Neural crest cells are responsible solely for lens formation
Neural crest cells only form the retina

Neural crest cells contribute to the corneal stroma/endothelium, iris stroma, and trabecular meshwork, and their abnormal development can cause anterior segment dysgenesis syndromes associated with glaucoma
Neural crest cells have no role in anterior segment development
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.e: Neural crest-derived mesenchyme contributes extensively to anterior segment structures including corneal stroma/endothelium, iris stroma, and the trabecular meshwork; disruptions in this developmental process underlie anterior segment dysgenesis syndromes, which carry an increased risk of glaucoma.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The pituitary gland is located within which bony structure of the skull base?
o: Sella turcica of the sphenoid bone
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The pituitary gland sits within the sella turcica, a saddle-shaped depression in the sphenoid bone.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) develops embryologically from which structure?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The anterior pituitary develops from Rathke's pouch, an upward invagination of oral ectoderm, distinguishing it embryologically from the neuroectoderm-derived posterior pituitary.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which histological cell type of the anterior pituitary secretes growth hormone?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Somatotrophs, the most numerous anterior pituitary cell type, secrete growth hormone.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which anterior pituitary cell type secretes prolactin?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Lactotrophs secrete prolactin, which stimulates milk production in the mammary gland.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The thyroid gland is located anterior to which structures in the neck?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The thyroid gland straddles the trachea, with its isthmus typically overlying the second to fourth tracheal rings, and lobes extending laterally alongside the larynx/trachea.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The thyroid gland develops embryologically from which structure, explaining the potential for ectopic thyroid tissue along its migration path?
o: A downgrowth from the foramen cecum at the base of the tongue, migrating via the thyroglossal duct
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The thyroid originates from an endodermal downgrowth at the foramen cecum of the tongue, descending via the thyroglossal duct to its final pretracheal position; remnants along this path can form ectopic thyroid tissue or thyroglossal duct cysts.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Thyroid follicular cells, which produce thyroid hormone, are histologically arranged around which central storage substance?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Thyroid follicles consist of a single layer of follicular cells surrounding colloid, which stores thyroglobulin, the precursor protein for thyroid hormone synthesis.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid, located between follicles, secrete which hormone?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Parafollicular C cells, derived embryologically from the ultimobranchial body (fourth/fifth pharyngeal pouch, neural crest origin), secrete calcitonin, which lowers serum calcium.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The parathyroid glands, typically four in number, are most commonly located in which anatomical position?
o: Within the mediastinum in all individuals
On the posterior surface of the thyroid gland
Within the thyroid gland parenchyma always
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The parathyroid glands are typically found on the posterior surface of the thyroid gland, though ectopic locations (including mediastinal) occur due to variable embryological descent.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The superior parathyroid glands develop from which pharyngeal pouch, while the inferior parathyroid glands develop from another, explaining their variable final positions?
o: Both develop from the same pouch
Superior from the fourth pouch; inferior from the third pouch
Neither develops from a pharyngeal pouch
Superior from the third pouch; inferior from the fourth pouch
Superior from the second pouch; inferior from the fourth pouch
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The superior parathyroids derive from the fourth pharyngeal pouch, while the inferior parathyroids derive from the third pouch (alongside the thymus), and their differing migration distances explain the more variable location of the inferior glands.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The adrenal cortex is divided into three histological zones; which zone is the outermost and secretes mineralocorticoids?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The zona glomerulosa, the outermost cortical zone, secretes mineralocorticoids (primarily aldosterone).

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The zona fasciculata, the middle and largest zone of the adrenal cortex, primarily secretes which hormone class?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The zona fasciculata is the primary site of glucocorticoid (cortisol) synthesis, under regulation by ACTH.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The zona reticularis, the innermost cortical zone, primarily secretes which hormone class?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The zona reticularis primarily produces adrenal androgens such as dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA).

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The adrenal medulla, embryologically derived from neural crest cells, secretes which hormones predominantly?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The adrenal medulla, composed of modified sympathetic postganglionic neurons (chromaffin cells), secretes catecholamines, predominantly epinephrine.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The pancreatic islets of Langerhans are histologically distinguished from the surrounding exocrine pancreatic tissue by which feature?
o: Identical staining characteristics to exocrine tissue
Clusters of pale-staining endocrine cells scattered within the darker-staining exocrine acinar tissue
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Pancreatic islets appear as pale-staining clusters of endocrine cells scattered among the more numerous, darker-staining exocrine acinar cells.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Within the pancreatic islets, beta cells (which secrete insulin) are typically located in which position relative to other islet cell types?
o: Centrally, comprising the majority of islet cell mass, with alpha cells more peripheral
Randomly distributed with no characteristic pattern
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Beta cells typically occupy the central portion of the islet and constitute the majority of islet cells, with alpha (glucagon-secreting) cells more peripherally located.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The pineal gland, located in the epithalamus, is histologically notable for containing which calcified structures with age, useful as a radiological midline marker?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The pineal gland accumulates calcified corpora arenacea ('brain sand') with age, useful radiologically as a midline marker on skull imaging.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which hormone-producing cells are found in the posterior pituitary, distinguishing its function from hormone synthesis occurring in the anterior pituitary?
o: The posterior pituitary has no hormonal function
The posterior pituitary contains hormone-synthesizing cells, similar to the anterior pituitary
The posterior pituitary contains axon terminals of hypothalamic neurons (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei) that store and release ADH and oxytocin, synthesized in the hypothalamus
The posterior pituitary produces thyroid-stimulating hormone
The posterior pituitary produces growth hormone
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Unlike the anterior pituitary, the posterior pituitary does not synthesize its own hormones; it stores and releases ADH and oxytocin that are synthesized in hypothalamic neurons (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei) and transported down their axons.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system is a specialized vascular network connecting which two structures, enabling local, high-concentration hormone delivery?
o: The hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary, carrying releasing and inhibiting hormones
The hypothalamus and the posterior pituitary via direct neural connection only
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system carries hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones directly to the anterior pituitary at high local concentrations, allowing precise regulation of anterior pituitary hormone secretion.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which of the following describes the classic histological appearance of a pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla?
o: Nests of chromaffin cells ('zellballen' pattern) with abundant vascularity
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Pheochromocytomas classically show a 'zellballen' (cell-ball) pattern of chromaffin cells arranged in nests surrounded by a rich vascular network, consistent with their neuroendocrine origin.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which of the following endocrine glands' histological structure includes concentric layers of keratinized epithelial cells known as Hassall's corpuscles?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Hassall's corpuscles, concentric whorls of keratinized epithelial reticular cells, are a histological hallmark of the thymic medulla.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which of the following best describes the relationship between the thymus and endocrine function, despite not being classically described alongside the classic endocrine glands?
o: The thymus has no relationship to the endocrine system
The thymus is purely an exocrine gland
The thymus is part of the adrenal cortex
The thymus secretes hormones (e.g., thymosin) important for T lymphocyte maturation, giving it an endocrine-like function alongside its primary immunological role
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: While primarily known for its role in T lymphocyte maturation, the thymus also secretes hormone-like factors (e.g., thymosin, thymopoietin) supporting this maturation process, giving it a degree of endocrine function.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The ovaries and testes are considered which type of gland, given their dual role in gamete production and hormone secretion?
o: Purely endocrine glands with no exocrine function
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The gonads (ovaries and testes) function as mixed glands, with an exocrine component (gamete production and release) and an endocrine component (steroid hormone secretion).

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Leydig cells of the testis, located in the interstitial tissue between seminiferous tubules, primarily secrete which hormone?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Leydig (interstitial) cells secrete testosterone in response to LH stimulation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Sertoli cells, located within the seminiferous tubules, perform which key functions?
o: Support and nourishment of developing sperm cells, secretion of inhibin, and formation of the blood-testis barrier
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Sertoli cells provide structural and nutritional support to developing spermatozoa, secrete inhibin (feedback regulation of FSH), and form tight junctions constituting the blood-testis barrier.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Granulosa cells of the ovarian follicle primarily secrete which hormone under the influence of FSH?
o: Estrogen (via aromatization of androgens supplied by theca cells)
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Granulosa cells, stimulated by FSH, aromatize androgens (supplied by neighboring theca cells) into estrogen, a key step in follicular development.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Theca cells of the ovarian follicle, under LH stimulation, primarily provide which substrate to granulosa cells for estrogen synthesis?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: LH-stimulated theca cells produce androgens, which diffuse to adjacent granulosa cells for aromatization into estrogen, illustrating the 'two-cell, two-gonadotropin' theory of ovarian steroidogenesis.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The corpus luteum, formed from the ruptured follicle after ovulation, primarily secretes which hormone to support early pregnancy if fertilization occurs?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and estrogen), maintaining the endometrium and supporting early pregnancy until placental steroidogenesis takes over.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which of the following best describes the histological zonation of the adrenal cortex from outer to inner?
o: Zona reticularis, zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata
Zona reticularis, zona fasciculata, zona glomerulosa
Zona fasciculata, zona glomerulosa, zona reticularis
Zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, zona reticularis
Zona glomerulosa, zona reticularis, zona fasciculata
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: From the capsule inward, the adrenal cortex is organized into the zona glomerulosa (mineralocorticoids), zona fasciculata (glucocorticoids), and zona reticularis (androgens).

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which cell type of the thyroid gland is responsible for calcitonin secretion?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Parafollicular or C cells, located between follicles or within the follicular basement membrane, secrete calcitonin in response to hypercalcemia.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which of the following best describes the histological appearance of thyroid follicles on light microscopy?
o: Flattened squamous cells arranged in sheets
Solid clusters of cells with no lumen
Spherical structures lined by a single layer of follicular epithelium surrounding a central colloid-filled lumen
Branching tubular glands with striated ducts
Cords of cells separated by sinusoidal capillaries only, without any lumen
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Thyroid follicles are spherical, each lined by a single layer of cuboidal-to-squamous follicular cells enclosing a colloid-filled lumen containing thyroglobulin.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The parathyroid glands are typically located in which anatomical position?
o: Lateral to the common carotid artery
Within the substance of the thyroid isthmus
On the posterior surface of the thyroid gland, usually two superior and two inferior glands
Anterior to the trachea below the cricoid cartilage
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The parathyroid glands are typically four small glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes, though their number and precise location can vary.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which cell type of the parathyroid gland is chiefly responsible for parathyroid hormone (PTH) synthesis and secretion?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Chief (principal) cells are the predominant and primary hormone-secreting cells of the parathyroid gland, synthesizing and releasing PTH.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which of the following best describes the blood supply pattern of the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis)?
o: No blood supply; it is avascular
A hypophyseal portal venous system carrying hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting hormones from the median eminence
Supply exclusively from the posterior communicating artery
Direct arterial supply only, with no venous portal system
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The anterior pituitary lacks direct hypothalamic neural input and instead receives hypothalamic regulatory hormones via the hypophyseal portal venous system, which carries releasing and inhibiting hormones from the median eminence.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) is best described histologically as composed mainly of which structures?
o: Unmyelinated axon terminals of hypothalamic neurons (from supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei) along with pituicytes
Secretory epithelial cells arranged in cords
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The posterior pituitary is neural tissue, consisting of axon terminals from hypothalamic magnocellular neurons (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei) that store and release oxytocin and vasopressin, supported by glial-like pituicytes.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which of the following pancreatic islet cell types is located centrally within the islet of Langerhans and is the most numerous?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Beta cells, which secrete insulin, are the most numerous islet cell type and are typically located centrally within the islet of Langerhans.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which pancreatic islet cell type secretes glucagon and is typically located peripherally within the islet?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Alpha cells secrete glucagon and are usually located at the periphery of the islet of Langerhans, distinct from the centrally placed beta cells.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which of the following best describes the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla?
o: Modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons that secrete catecholamines directly into the bloodstream
Cells structurally identical to zona fasciculata cells
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are derived from neural crest tissue and function as modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons, releasing catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) directly into the circulation rather than at a synapse.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: The pineal gland is best described as being composed predominantly of which cell type?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: The pineal gland is composed mainly of pinealocytes, specialized neuroendocrine cells that synthesize and secrete melatonin, along with supporting glial cells.

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.s: Which of the following structures develops embryologically from Rathke's pouch, an upward evagination of the primitive oral ectoderm?
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.e: Rathke's pouch, an ectodermal outgrowth from the roof of the primitive oral cavity, gives rise to the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis), while the posterior pituitary arises from a neural downgrowth of the diencephalon.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Growth hormone release from the anterior pituitary is stimulated by which hypothalamic hormone?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: GHRH from the hypothalamus stimulates somatotroph secretion of growth hormone, while somatostatin inhibits it.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Most of growth hormone's growth-promoting effects on bone and tissue are mediated indirectly via which factor produced primarily by the liver?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Growth hormone stimulates hepatic (and local tissue) production of IGF-1, which mediates most of GH's anabolic and growth-promoting actions.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Excess growth hormone secretion in adults, after epiphyseal plate closure, causes which clinical condition?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Excess GH after epiphyseal closure causes acromegaly, characterized by enlargement of bones (especially hands, feet, jaw) and soft tissues, without an increase in height.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Excess growth hormone secretion in children, before epiphyseal plate closure, causes which condition?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Excess GH in children before epiphyseal closure causes gigantism, with excessive linear growth.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Thyroid hormone synthesis requires which essential dietary element?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Iodine is an essential component of thyroid hormones (T3 and T4); dietary iodine deficiency impairs thyroid hormone synthesis.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which enzyme, expressed on the apical membrane of thyroid follicular cells, catalyzes iodination of tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Thyroid peroxidase catalyzes both the oxidation of iodide and its incorporation (organification) onto tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin, key steps in thyroid hormone synthesis.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which thyroid hormone, T3 or T4, is more biologically active at target tissues, despite T4 being secreted in much larger quantities?
o: T3 (triiodothyronine) is more biologically active, largely formed by peripheral deiodination of T4
Neither is active without conversion to T2
T4 is more active than T3
Only T4 has any biological activity
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Although T4 is secreted in greater quantity, T3 is the more biologically active form, mostly generated by peripheral deiodination of T4 in target tissues.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which thyroid function test result would be expected in primary hypothyroidism (thyroid gland failure)?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Primary hypothyroidism (thyroid gland failure) results in low thyroid hormone output, with compensatory elevation of TSH due to reduced negative feedback.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Graves' disease, an autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism, results from autoantibodies that do what?
o: Stimulate the TSH receptor, causing excess thyroid hormone production
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Graves' disease involves thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) that activate the TSH receptor, causing unregulated excess thyroid hormone synthesis and release.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which hormone, secreted by the parathyroid glands, is the primary regulator of minute-to-minute serum calcium concentration?
o: Vitamin D exclusively without PTH involvement
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: PTH is the principal hormone regulating serum calcium, acting on bone, kidney, and indirectly the intestine (via calcitriol) to raise calcium levels in response to hypocalcemia.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Cortisol, the primary glucocorticoid, has which overall metabolic effect during stress?
o: Promotes glycogen synthesis and lowers blood glucose
Has no effect on glucose metabolism
Stimulates insulin-like anabolic effects on protein
Promotes gluconeogenesis, raises blood glucose, and has anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive effects
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Cortisol raises blood glucose via gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, promotes protein catabolism, and exerts significant anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects, particularly important during stress.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Addison's disease, primary adrenal insufficiency, results in deficiency of which hormones?
o: Both cortisol and aldosterone (and adrenal androgens)
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) affects the entire adrenal cortex, causing deficiency of cortisol, aldosterone, and adrenal androgens.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Cushing's syndrome, resulting from excess cortisol, classically presents with which combination of findings?
o: Central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, hypertension, and hyperglycemia
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Cushing's syndrome classically presents with central obesity, moon facies, buffalo hump, hypertension, hyperglycemia, and other features of glucocorticoid excess.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Insulin, secreted by pancreatic beta cells, has which overall metabolic effect?
o: Promotes catabolism and raises blood glucose
Has no effect on fat metabolism
Promotes anabolism, cellular glucose uptake, and lowers blood glucose
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Insulin promotes anabolic processes including cellular glucose uptake (especially in muscle and adipose tissue), glycogen synthesis, and lipogenesis, overall lowering blood glucose.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Type 1 diabetes mellitus results primarily from which pathological process?
o: Peripheral insulin resistance with preserved beta cell function
Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, causing absolute insulin deficiency
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells, leading to absolute insulin deficiency requiring exogenous insulin replacement.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is primarily characterized by which pathophysiological process, at least initially?
o: Complete absence of insulin secretion from onset
Peripheral insulin resistance with relative (and progressive) beta cell dysfunction
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Type 2 diabetes typically begins with peripheral insulin resistance, with beta cells initially compensating via increased insulin secretion before progressive beta cell dysfunction develops.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Glucagon, secreted by pancreatic alpha cells in response to hypoglycemia, exerts its effects primarily on which organ?
o: Pancreas itself, in an autocrine manner only
Adipose tissue exclusively without hepatic effects
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Glucagon primarily targets the liver, stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis to raise blood glucose during fasting or hypoglycemia.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which hormone, produced by adipose tissue, signals satiety to the hypothalamus and is generally found at levels proportional to body fat stores?
o: Adiponectin exclusively regulates only glucose, not satiety
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Leptin, secreted by adipocytes in proportion to fat mass, signals satiety to the hypothalamus, helping regulate long-term energy balance.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Ghrelin, often called the 'hunger hormone,' is primarily secreted by which organ?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Ghrelin is secreted mainly by the stomach, particularly when empty, stimulating appetite and growth hormone release.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), synthesized in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary, primarily acts on which target organ?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: ADH acts on the renal collecting duct, promoting water reabsorption via aquaporin-2 channel insertion, in response to increased plasma osmolarity or decreased blood volume.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Oxytocin, released from the posterior pituitary, stimulates which two key physiological processes?
o: Water reabsorption and blood pressure regulation
Milk ejection (let-down reflex) and uterine contraction during labor
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Oxytocin stimulates myoepithelial cell contraction in the breast (milk ejection reflex) and uterine smooth muscle contraction, particularly important during labor and breastfeeding.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which hormone, secreted by the anterior pituitary, stimulates spermatogenesis in males by acting on Sertoli cells?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support and stimulate spermatogenesis, while LH acts on Leydig cells to stimulate testosterone production.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which hormone, secreted by the anterior pituitary, triggers ovulation via a mid-cycle surge?
o: Estrogen surge alone without LH involvement
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: A surge in LH, triggered by rising estrogen from the dominant follicle (positive feedback), precipitates ovulation approximately 36 hours later.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which hormone's excess secretion, often from a pituitary adenoma, classically causes galactorrhea and amenorrhea in women, and decreased libido in men?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Prolactinomas cause hyperprolactinemia, presenting with galactorrhea and menstrual irregularities/amenorrhea in women, and decreased libido/erectile dysfunction in men, partly via suppression of GnRH.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which hormone axis regulates cortisol secretion, involving sequential release of hormones from the hypothalamus, pituitary, and adrenal cortex?
o: Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis: CRH, then ACTH, then cortisol
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: The HPA axis involves hypothalamic CRH stimulating pituitary ACTH release, which in turn stimulates adrenal cortisol secretion, with negative feedback at multiple levels.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which of the following best describes the physiological basis of the dexamethasone suppression test, used in evaluating suspected Cushing's syndrome?
o: Dexamethasone, a synthetic glucocorticoid, should suppress ACTH and endogenous cortisol via negative feedback in normal individuals; failure to suppress suggests autonomous cortisol production
The test evaluates thyroid function exclusively
Dexamethasone has no effect on the HPA axis
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: In healthy individuals, exogenous dexamethasone suppresses pituitary ACTH secretion via negative feedback, lowering cortisol; failure of this suppression suggests autonomous cortisol overproduction (e.g., adrenal or ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor) in Cushing's syndrome.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which hormone, secreted in response to hypercalcemia, acts to lower serum calcium primarily by inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Calcitonin, secreted by thyroid parafollicular cells in response to hypercalcemia, inhibits osteoclast activity, lowering serum calcium, though its physiological role in humans is considered relatively minor compared to PTH.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which of the following best describes the physiological role of vitamin D (calcitriol) in calcium homeostasis, complementing PTH action?
o: It functions independently of PTH with no interaction
It increases intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate, and works synergistically with PTH to mobilize calcium from bone
It has no role in calcium regulation
It is produced only in the skin with no further activation needed
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Calcitriol (active vitamin D) enhances intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption and, together with PTH, promotes bone resorption when needed, working synergistically to maintain calcium homeostasis; it requires sequential hydroxylation in the liver and kidney for activation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which of the following best describes the negative feedback regulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis?
o: Rising thyroid hormone levels stimulate further TSH secretion
There is no feedback regulation in this axis
Thyroid hormone has no effect on the pituitary or hypothalamus
Rising thyroid hormone levels inhibit hypothalamic TRH and pituitary TSH secretion
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Thyroid hormone (T3/T4) exerts negative feedback on both hypothalamic TRH and pituitary TSH secretion, maintaining thyroid hormone levels within a normal physiological range.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which of the following hormones is responsible for stimulating milk production (as opposed to milk ejection) in the postpartum period?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Prolactin stimulates milk synthesis and secretion by mammary alveolar cells, while oxytocin mediates the separate process of milk ejection (let-down reflex).

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which class of hormones typically acts via intracellular (cytoplasmic or nuclear) receptors rather than cell-surface receptors, owing to their lipophilic nature?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Steroid hormones and thyroid hormones are lipophilic and can cross the plasma membrane to bind intracellular receptors, which then act as transcription factors regulating gene expression, unlike hydrophilic peptide hormones that require surface receptors.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which second messenger system is most classically activated by glucagon binding to its hepatocyte receptor?
o: Cyclic AMP (cAMP) via Gs protein-coupled activation of adenylyl cyclase
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Glucagon binds Gs protein-coupled receptors on hepatocytes, activating adenylyl cyclase and raising intracellular cAMP, which activates protein kinase A to stimulate glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of negative feedback regulation in the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis?
o: Rising TSH suppresses hypothalamic TRH only, with no effect from thyroid hormone
There is no feedback regulation of this axis
Calcitonin, not thyroid hormone, provides the feedback signal
Rising circulating thyroid hormone (T3/T4) suppresses hypothalamic TRH and pituitary TSH secretion
Thyroid hormone stimulates further TRH and TSH release
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Circulating thyroid hormones exert negative feedback at both the hypothalamus (suppressing TRH) and anterior pituitary (suppressing TSH), maintaining a tightly regulated set point of circulating thyroid hormone.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which hormone is primarily responsible for stimulating hepatic and renal gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis in response to hypoglycemia?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Glucagon, secreted by pancreatic alpha cells in response to falling blood glucose, promotes hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, raising blood glucose.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which of the following best explains why growth hormone (GH) exerts many of its growth-promoting effects indirectly rather than directly?
o: GH directly enters the nucleus of target cells as a lipophilic hormone
GH has no growth-promoting effects at all
GH acts only on bone, with no hepatic involvement
GH is entirely inactive until converted to cortisol
GH stimulates hepatic (and local tissue) production of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), which mediates most anabolic and growth effects
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Growth hormone stimulates the liver (and other tissues) to produce IGF-1, which mediates most of the anabolic, growth-promoting actions traditionally attributed to GH itself, in addition to some direct GH effects.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which of the following best describes the primary physiological trigger for aldosterone secretion from the zona glomerulosa?
o: ACTH is the sole and primary long-term regulator
Angiotensin II (via the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system) and elevated plasma potassium
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Aldosterone secretion is primarily regulated by angiotensin II (generated via the renin-angiotensin system in response to low renal perfusion or low sodium) and directly by elevated plasma potassium, promoting renal sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which of the following hormones raises blood glucose primarily by antagonizing insulin's peripheral action and promoting hepatic glucose output, and is characteristically elevated in states of chronic stress?
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Cortisol is a counter-regulatory (insulin-antagonist) hormone that raises blood glucose via hepatic gluconeogenesis, reduced peripheral glucose uptake, and lipolysis, and its secretion increases during chronic physiological stress.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which of the following best describes the role of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in regulating thyroid hormone synthesis?
o: TSH binds receptors on thyroid follicular cells, stimulating iodide uptake, thyroglobulin synthesis, and release of T3/T4
TSH acts only on parafollicular cells to release calcitonin
TSH binds thyrotroph receptors, has no effect on the thyroid gland
TSH directly converts T4 to T3 in peripheral tissue only
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: TSH, secreted by anterior pituitary thyrotrophs, binds receptors on thyroid follicular cells, stimulating essentially every step of thyroid hormone synthesis and release, including iodide trapping and thyroglobulin processing.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which of the following best explains why insulin is described as an anabolic hormone?
o: It functions exclusively as a vasoconstrictor
It promotes only glucose breakdown, never storage
It has no effect on lipid metabolism
It stimulates only catabolic processes such as lipolysis and proteolysis
It promotes cellular uptake and storage of glucose (as glycogen), amino acids (as protein), and fatty acids (as triglycerides)
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Insulin promotes anabolism by facilitating cellular glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis, amino acid uptake and protein synthesis, and fatty acid uptake with triglyceride storage, while inhibiting catabolic pathways like glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, and lipolysis.

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.s: Which of the following best describes the physiological action of oxytocin during lactation?
o: It stimulates milk ejection (let-down) by causing contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding mammary alveoli, in response to suckling
It inhibits prolactin release, thereby stopping lactation
It stimulates milk synthesis directly within alveolar cells
It has no role in lactation
It stimulates uterine relaxation, unrelated to lactation
endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.e: Oxytocin, released from the posterior pituitary in response to suckling (a neuroendocrine reflex), causes contraction of myoepithelial cells around mammary alveoli, producing milk ejection (the let-down reflex).

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Spermatogenesis occurs within which structure of the testis?
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Spermatogenesis takes place within the seminiferous tubules, progressing from the basal to luminal compartment as sperm mature.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: The blood-testis barrier, formed by tight junctions between Sertoli cells, primarily serves which function?
o: Creates an immunologically privileged environment protecting developing sperm (which express novel antigens) from autoimmune attack
Prevents all blood flow to the testis
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: The blood-testis barrier isolates later stages of sperm development from the immune system, as haploid sperm express surface antigens not present during immune tolerance development, protecting against autoimmune destruction.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Following production in the seminiferous tubules, sperm mature and are stored primarily in which structure?
o: Vas deferens exclusively without storage in epididymis
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Sperm undergo final maturation (acquiring motility) and are stored in the epididymis before ejaculation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: During ejaculation, sperm travel from the epididymis through which structure to reach the ejaculatory duct?
o: Urethra directly without an intermediate structure
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: The vas deferens transports mature sperm from the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct during ejaculation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: The seminal vesicles contribute which major component to semen?
o: A fructose-rich alkaline fluid, providing energy substrate for sperm and contributing to the majority of semen volume
Acidic fluid rich in citric acid and zinc
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Seminal vesicle secretions, rich in fructose (an energy source for sperm) and prostaglandins, contribute the majority of semen volume.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: The prostate gland contributes which characteristic component to seminal fluid?
o: A thin, alkaline fluid containing prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and other enzymes aiding sperm motility and semen liquefaction
No fluid contribution, only sperm storage
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: The prostate secretes a thin, slightly alkaline fluid containing PSA and other proteolytic enzymes that help liquefy semen after ejaculation, aiding sperm motility.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), common in aging men, classically causes which urinary symptom due to its anatomical location?
o: Renal failure as the initial presentation always
Bladder outlet obstruction, causing urinary hesitancy, weak stream, and incomplete emptying
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: BPH involves enlargement of the periurethral (transition) zone of the prostate, which surrounds the urethra, causing bladder outlet obstruction with associated lower urinary tract symptoms.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Prostate cancer most commonly arises in which zone of the prostate gland?
o: Transition zone (the same zone typically affected by BPH)
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Most prostate cancers arise in the peripheral zone of the prostate, which is palpable on digital rectal examination, unlike the transition zone typically involved in BPH.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: The process of spermiogenesis refers to which specific stage of sperm development?
o: Sperm capacitation in the female tract
The transformation of round spermatids into elongated, motile spermatozoa
The initial mitotic proliferation of spermatogonia
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Spermiogenesis refers specifically to the morphological transformation of round spermatids into mature, motile spermatozoa, including acrosome and flagellum formation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Sperm capacitation, a final maturation step required for fertilization capability, occurs primarily where?
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Capacitation, involving biochemical changes to the sperm membrane enabling the acrosome reaction, occurs within the female reproductive tract after ejaculation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: The acrosome, a cap-like structure over the sperm head, is essential for which process during fertilization?
o: Penetrating the zona pellucida of the oocyte via release of hydrolytic enzymes (acrosome reaction)
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: The acrosome contains hydrolytic enzymes released during the acrosome reaction, enabling sperm penetration through the zona pellucida to reach and fuse with the oocyte membrane.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which cells provide the primary negative feedback signal (inhibin) to the anterior pituitary, helping regulate FSH secretion in males?
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Sertoli cells secrete inhibin, which selectively suppresses FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary, providing feedback regulation of spermatogenesis.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Testosterone exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis primarily by suppressing secretion of which hormones?
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Testosterone provides negative feedback at both the hypothalamus (suppressing GnRH) and pituitary (suppressing LH), regulating its own production.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which enzyme converts testosterone to the more potent androgen dihydrotestosterone (DHT) in target tissues such as the prostate and external genitalia?
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: 5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to DHT, which has greater androgen receptor affinity and is particularly important for prostate growth and external genitalia virilization.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: 5-alpha reductase deficiency in genetic males classically results in which clinical presentation at birth?
o: Complete female phenotype with normal female internal organs
Ambiguous genitalia, with virilization occurring at puberty due to testosterone's direct effects
Normal male genitalia with infertility only discovered later
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: 5-alpha reductase deficiency impairs DHT-dependent external genitalia virilization in utero, causing ambiguous genitalia at birth, though virilization can occur at puberty due to rising testosterone levels acting directly.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which cranial mechanism/pathway is primarily responsible for penile erection, involving parasympathetic-mediated release of nitric oxide?
o: Parasympathetic-mediated smooth muscle relaxation of the corpora cavernosa, allowing increased arterial inflow
Direct action of oxytocin on the penis
Hormonal control by testosterone alone, with no neural component
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Parasympathetic stimulation releases nitric oxide, causing smooth muscle relaxation within the corpora cavernosa and increased arterial blood inflow, resulting in erection.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which class of drugs, commonly used to treat erectile dysfunction, works by inhibiting the breakdown of cyclic GMP, prolonging smooth muscle relaxation?
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: PDE-5 inhibitors block the breakdown of cGMP (generated via nitric oxide signaling), prolonging smooth muscle relaxation and enhancing erectile response.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Varicocele, an abnormal dilation of the pampiniform venous plexus, occurs more commonly on which side and why?
o: Equally on both sides with no anatomical explanation
Neither side is more commonly affected
Right side, due to direct drainage into the IVC
Left side, because the left testicular vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein, creating higher venous pressure
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Varicoceles are more common on the left due to the left testicular vein's perpendicular drainage into the left renal vein (versus the right testicular vein's oblique drainage directly into the IVC), predisposing to higher venous pressure and reflux.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Cryptorchidism, the failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum, is associated with increased risk of which long-term complications if uncorrected?
o: Increased risk of prostate cancer specifically
Infertility and increased risk of testicular malignancy
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Undescended testes, if not surgically corrected, carry increased risks of impaired spermatogenesis (infertility) and testicular malignancy, related to the higher intra-abdominal temperature affecting testicular tissue.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which of the following structures directly transports spermatozoa from the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct?
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: The vas deferens is a muscular duct that transports mature spermatozoa from the tail of the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct, where it joins the seminal vesicle duct.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which cells within the seminiferous tubules provide structural and nutritive support to developing spermatogenic cells and form the blood-testis barrier?
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Sertoli cells, located within the seminiferous tubules, support and nourish developing germ cells, secrete androgen-binding protein and inhibin, and form tight junctions constituting the blood-testis barrier.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which cells located in the interstitial tissue between seminiferous tubules are primarily responsible for testosterone production?
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Leydig cells, located in the interstitium between seminiferous tubules, produce testosterone in response to luteinizing hormone (LH) stimulation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which of the following accessory glands contributes the majority of the volume of semen, providing fructose-rich secretions that nourish spermatozoa?
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: The seminal vesicles contribute approximately 60-70% of seminal fluid volume, rich in fructose (an energy substrate for sperm) and prostaglandins.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which of the following best describes the primary contribution of the prostate gland to semen?
o: The majority of seminal fluid volume
A thin, alkaline, enzyme-rich fluid (including prostate-specific antigen) that helps liquefy semen and neutralize vaginal acidity
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Prostatic secretions are thin and alkaline, containing enzymes such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) that aid in liquefying coagulated semen, and help neutralize the acidic vaginal environment.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which hormone directly stimulates Leydig cells to synthesize and secrete testosterone?
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: LH, secreted by anterior pituitary gonadotrophs, binds receptors on Leydig cells, stimulating testosterone synthesis, analogous to LH's action on ovarian theca cells.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which hormone acts primarily on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis?
o: Testosterone alone, with no pituitary input
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: FSH acts on Sertoli cells, stimulating androgen-binding protein production and supporting the environment necessary for spermatogenesis, working together with intratesticular testosterone.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which of the following best describes the process of spermiogenesis?
o: The maturation of sperm within the epididymis
The process by which testosterone is synthesized
The differentiation of round spermatids into elongated, motile spermatozoa without further cell division
The meiotic division producing secondary spermatocytes
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Spermiogenesis is the final stage of spermatogenesis in which round spermatids undergo morphological transformation (acrosome formation, flagellum development, nuclear condensation) into mature spermatozoa, without additional cell division.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Where does functional maturation of spermatozoa (acquisition of motility) primarily occur after they leave the testis?
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Spermatozoa leaving the testis are structurally complete but functionally immature; they acquire progressive motility and fertilizing capacity during their transit and storage in the epididymis.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which of the following best describes capacitation of spermatozoa?
o: A series of physiological changes occurring in the female reproductive tract that enable sperm to fertilize an oocyte
A process occurring in the prostate gland before ejaculation
The initial formation of the acrosome in the testis
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Capacitation refers to physiological and biochemical changes to the sperm membrane that occur within the female reproductive tract, required before sperm can undergo the acrosome reaction and fertilize an oocyte.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which of the following best describes the arterial supply to the testis?
o: Branches of the femoral artery exclusively
Branches of the inferior mesenteric artery
Testicular arteries arising from the internal iliac artery
Branches of the internal pudendal artery only
Testicular arteries arising directly from the abdominal aorta, just below the renal arteries
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: The testicular arteries arise directly from the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries, reflecting the testis's embryological origin high in the abdomen before its descent into the scrotum.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which venous drainage pattern is characteristic of the testis and is clinically relevant to the higher incidence of left-sided varicocele?
o: The left testicular vein drains into the azygos vein
The right testicular vein drains into the inferior vena cava directly, while the left testicular vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein, creating higher resistance
Both testicular veins drain directly and symmetrically into the inferior vena cava
There is no difference between right and left venous drainage
Both testicular veins drain into the renal veins symmetrically
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: The right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava at an oblique angle, while the left testicular vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein, creating relatively higher venous pressure and predisposing to left-sided varicocele.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which structure forms a temperature-regulating countercurrent heat exchange mechanism within the spermatic cord, helping maintain testicular temperature below core body temperature?
o: Pampiniform plexus surrounding the testicular artery
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: The pampiniform venous plexus surrounds the testicular artery within the spermatic cord, functioning as a countercurrent heat exchanger that cools arterial blood before it reaches the testis, helping maintain the lower temperature required for spermatogenesis.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which of the following best describes the role of the cremaster muscle?
o: It elevates the testis toward the body in response to cold or the cremasteric reflex, helping regulate testicular temperature
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: The cremaster muscle, derived from the internal oblique muscle, reflexively elevates the testis toward the body (e.g., in cold temperatures or with the cremasteric reflex), contributing to testicular thermoregulation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which of the following best describes erectile physiology of the penis?
o: Erection results purely from increased venous outflow with no arterial component
Parasympathetic stimulation releases nitric oxide, causing smooth muscle relaxation in the corpora cavernosa and increased arterial inflow leading to erection
Erection is mediated exclusively by somatic motor neurons
Erection is a passive process requiring no autonomic input
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Erection is primarily a parasympathetically mediated event: nitric oxide release causes smooth muscle relaxation in the corpora cavernosa, increasing arterial inflow and compressing venous outflow, producing engorgement and rigidity.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which of the following best describes the process of emission during male sexual response?
o: Sympathetically mediated contraction of the vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and prostate, delivering semen into the prostatic urethra
Contraction of the bladder detrusor muscle alone
Passive dribbling of seminal fluid with no muscular contraction
A process occurring exclusively within the testis
A parasympathetically mediated process identical to erection
