endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Emission is a sympathetically mediated process involving peristaltic contraction of the vas deferens and secretion/contraction of the seminal vesicles and prostate, delivering semen into the prostatic urethra prior to ejaculation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which of the following best explains why the testes normally descend into the scrotum during fetal development?
o: The abdominal cavity is too small to accommodate the testes
Descent is required for testosterone synthesis to begin at all
The scrotal location maintains testicular temperature approximately 2-3°C below core body temperature, which is optimal for spermatogenesis
Descent occurs purely for mechanical protection with no thermal benefit
The scrotal location has no thermoregulatory significance
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Spermatogenesis is temperature-sensitive and functions optimally at temperatures below core body temperature; scrotal location, aided by mechanisms like the pampiniform plexus and cremaster muscle, maintains this cooler environment.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which of the following hormones, when administered in excess or produced by an exogenous source, exerts negative feedback that can suppress endogenous LH/FSH secretion and impair spermatogenesis?
o: Testosterone (via negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis)
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Testosterone (and its metabolites) exerts negative feedback on hypothalamic GnRH and pituitary LH/FSH secretion; excess exogenous testosterone can suppress the HPG axis and paradoxically impair spermatogenesis by reducing endogenous LH-driven Leydig cell stimulation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which of the following best describes inhibin's physiological role in male reproductive physiology?
o: It is secreted by Sertoli cells and selectively suppresses FSH secretion via negative feedback on the anterior pituitary
It is the primary androgen responsible for secondary sexual characteristics
It has no feedback role in the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis
It is secreted by Leydig cells and stimulates LH secretion
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: Inhibin, secreted by Sertoli cells in response to the state of spermatogenesis, selectively suppresses FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary, providing feedback regulation distinct from testosterone's broader HPG axis feedback.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which of the following structures is the direct continuation of the vas deferens as it joins the duct of the seminal vesicle?
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: The ejaculatory duct is formed by the union of the vas deferens and the duct of the seminal vesicle, and it passes through the prostate to open into the prostatic urethra.

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.s: Which of the following best describes the tunica vaginalis of the testis?
o: The outermost layer of the scrotal skin
A closed peritoneal sac derived from the processus vaginalis, covering the anterior and lateral surfaces of the testis
A muscular layer responsible for testicular elevation
The duct system connecting the testis to the epididymis
A dense fibrous capsule directly surrounding the seminiferous tubules
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.e: The tunica vaginalis is a closed peritoneal sac, a remnant of the processus vaginalis that accompanied testicular descent, covering the anterior and lateral aspects of the testis and providing a smooth serosal surface; a persistent connection to the peritoneal cavity can allow fluid accumulation (hydrocele).

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: The ovarian follicular phase of the menstrual cycle is primarily characterized by which hormonal pattern?
o: Constant hormone levels with no variation
Rising estrogen (from developing follicles) with relatively low progesterone
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: During the follicular phase, developing ovarian follicles secrete increasing amounts of estrogen, while progesterone remains relatively low until after ovulation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which structure secretes progesterone predominantly during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle?
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: After ovulation, the corpus luteum forms from the ruptured follicle and secretes progesterone (and some estrogen) during the luteal phase.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates into which structure, with an associated drop in progesterone triggering menstruation?
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: In the absence of fertilization/hCG support, the corpus luteum regresses into a fibrous scar called the corpus albicans, with the resultant drop in progesterone triggering endometrial shedding (menstruation).

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: During pregnancy, which hormone, produced by the syncytiotrophoblast, maintains the corpus luteum's progesterone secretion during early pregnancy?
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: hCG, structurally similar to LH, maintains corpus luteum function and progesterone secretion during early pregnancy until placental steroidogenesis becomes sufficient (around 8-10 weeks).

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: The endometrium undergoes cyclical changes; which layer is shed during menstruation while the deeper layer regenerates the endometrium each cycle?
o: Stratum functionale is shed; stratum basale regenerates the endometrium
Stratum basale is shed; stratum functionale regenerates
Neither layer changes during the cycle
The entire endometrium including basale regenerates from the cervix
Both layers are completely shed and regenerated from the myometrium
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The stratum functionale is shed during menstruation, while the underlying stratum basale is retained and regenerates the functional layer during the subsequent cycle.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Fertilization of the oocyte by sperm typically occurs in which part of the female reproductive tract?
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: Fertilization typically occurs in the ampulla, the widest and longest portion of the uterine tube, following ovulation and sperm transport.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: The fertilized zygote undergoes cleavage divisions while traveling through the uterine tube, typically implanting in the uterine wall at approximately which day post-fertilization?
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: Implantation of the blastocyst into the endometrium typically occurs around day 6-7 post-fertilization, after the morula has developed into a blastocyst during transit through the uterine tube.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which uterine ligament contains the ovarian vessels and suspends the ovary from the lateral pelvic wall?
o: Broad ligament exclusively without vascular contents
Suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament)
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament) carries the ovarian artery, vein, and nerves, connecting the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: The round ligament of the uterus is the embryological remnant of which structure, analogous to the male gubernaculum?
o: The gubernaculum (representing the homologous structure to the male gubernaculum testis)
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The round ligament is homologous to the male gubernaculum, representing a remnant of the structure that, in males, guides testicular descent; in females it extends from the uterus through the inguinal canal to the labia majora.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: The uterine (fallopian) tubes are divided into four parts; which part is closest to the ovary and features fimbriae to capture the released oocyte?
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The infundibulum, the funnel-shaped distal end of the uterine tube, bears fimbriae that help capture the oocyte released at ovulation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: The cervix produces mucus whose consistency changes throughout the menstrual cycle under hormonal influence; which type of mucus is produced around ovulation, facilitating sperm transport?
o: Thick, viscous mucus impeding sperm passage
No mucus production at any point in the cycle
Only progesterone-dominant thick mucus throughout the cycle
Thin, watery, elastic ('spinnbarkeit') mucus under estrogen influence, facilitating sperm penetration
Mucus production only occurs during menstruation
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: High estrogen levels around ovulation produce thin, clear, elastic cervical mucus (with high spinnbarkeit) that facilitates sperm penetration and survival, in contrast to thick, hostile mucus during the luteal phase under progesterone influence.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: The vaginal epithelium undergoes cyclical changes under hormonal influence; estrogen promotes which change in the vaginal epithelium?
o: No change occurs with hormonal fluctuation
Proliferation and cornification (maturation), increasing glycogen content
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: Estrogen promotes proliferation and maturation (cornification) of the vaginal squamous epithelium, increasing glycogen content that supports lactobacilli and vaginal acidity.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Lactobacilli in the normal vaginal flora contribute to vaginal health primarily by which mechanism?
o: Neutralizing vaginal pH to be alkaline
Producing lactic acid from glycogen, maintaining an acidic vaginal pH that inhibits pathogenic organism overgrowth
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: Lactobacilli metabolize glycogen (abundant in estrogen-primed vaginal epithelium) into lactic acid, maintaining an acidic vaginal environment that helps prevent overgrowth of pathogenic organisms.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Menopause is defined clinically as the permanent cessation of menstruation, resulting primarily from which physiological change?
o: Depletion of ovarian follicles, causing declining estrogen production
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: Menopause results from age-related depletion of the finite ovarian follicular reserve, leading to declining estrogen production and eventual cessation of ovulation and menstruation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which hormonal pattern is characteristic of menopause, given the loss of negative feedback from declining ovarian estrogen production?
o: Low FSH and LH with low estrogen
High estrogen with normal FSH and LH
Normal FSH and LH with low estrogen
High FSH and LH, low estrogen
Low FSH and LH, high estrogen
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: Reduced ovarian estrogen production removes negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, resulting in markedly elevated FSH and LH levels characteristic of menopause.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes the process of oogenesis, particularly regarding the timing of meiotic completion, distinguishing it from spermatogenesis?
o: Meiosis in oogenesis is completed entirely within the fallopian tube before ovulation
Oogenesis begins only at puberty with no prenatal component
Oogenesis is completed entirely before birth, identical to spermatogenesis timing
Oocytes arrest in meiosis I (prophase) before birth and only complete meiosis I at ovulation, with meiosis II completing only upon fertilization
Oogenesis produces four functional gametes per meiotic cycle, identical to spermatogenesis
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: Oocytes arrest in prophase of meiosis I before birth, resuming and completing meiosis I just before ovulation (producing a secondary oocyte and first polar body), with meiosis II completing only if fertilization occurs.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best explains why oogenesis typically produces only one functional gamete (plus polar bodies) per meiotic cycle, unlike spermatogenesis which produces four functional sperm?
o: All four products of oogenesis are functional oocytes
Oogenesis does not involve meiotic division at all
Polar bodies eventually develop into additional oocytes
Unequal cytoplasmic division during meiosis, concentrating cytoplasm and nutrients into a single large oocyte while polar bodies receive minimal cytoplasm
This is incorrect; both processes produce four functional gametes
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: Asymmetric cytoplasmic division during oogenesis concentrates the bulk of cytoplasm and organelles into a single large, nutrient-rich oocyte, while the genetic material not retained is discarded into small, non-functional polar bodies.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following describes the pouch of Douglas (rectouterine pouch), an important pelvic anatomical landmark?
o: The space between the ovaries and fallopian tubes
The space anterior to the bladder
A structure found only in males
The space between the bladder and uterus
The most posterior and inferior extent of the peritoneal cavity in females, between the rectum and uterus
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) is the most dependent portion of the peritoneal cavity in females, located between the rectum and posterior uterine wall, and is a common site for fluid or pus accumulation and for culdocentesis.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes the physiological changes in basal body temperature across the menstrual cycle, useful for fertility tracking?
o: Basal body temperature remains constant throughout the cycle
A sustained rise in basal body temperature occurs after ovulation, due to the thermogenic effect of progesterone
Temperature falls after ovulation and remains low until menstruation
There is no relationship between hormones and basal body temperature
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: Progesterone, secreted after ovulation by the corpus luteum, has a mild thermogenic effect, causing a sustained rise (typically 0.3-0.5°C) in basal body temperature during the luteal phase, useful for retrospectively estimating ovulation timing.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes the primary function of the fimbriae of the uterine (fallopian) tube?
o: To anchor the ovary to the pelvic wall
To sweep the ovulated oocyte into the tube's ampulla for potential fertilization
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The fimbriae are finger-like projections at the infundibulum of the uterine tube that create currents to capture the ovulated oocyte and sweep it into the tube, where fertilization typically occurs in the ampulla.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Fertilization of the oocyte by spermatozoa most commonly occurs in which portion of the female reproductive tract?
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: Fertilization most commonly occurs in the ampulla, the widest and longest portion of the uterine tube, shortly after ovulation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which layer of the uterus undergoes cyclical shedding during menstruation?
o: Functional layer of the endometrium (stratum functionalis)
Basal layer of the endometrium (stratum basalis)
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The functional layer (stratum functionalis) of the endometrium proliferates and is shed cyclically in response to hormonal changes, while the basal layer regenerates it each cycle.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which ovarian structure secretes progesterone predominantly during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle?
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: After ovulation, the ruptured follicle transforms into the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone (and some estrogen) to support the luteal phase and prepare the endometrium for potential implantation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes the fate of the corpus luteum in the absence of pregnancy?
o: It converts into a corpus hemorrhagicum permanently
It persists indefinitely, continuing progesterone secretion
It becomes the site of implantation
It degenerates into the corpus albicans as progesterone and estrogen levels fall, triggering menstruation
It transforms directly into a new primordial follicle
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: In the absence of fertilization/implantation (and the resulting hCG signal), the corpus luteum regresses into the corpus albicans (a fibrous scar) after about 14 days, and the associated fall in progesterone and estrogen triggers endometrial shedding (menstruation).

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which hormone from the developing embryo/trophoblast maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy, preventing its regression?
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: hCG, secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast of the developing conceptus, has LH-like activity and maintains the corpus luteum's progesterone secretion during early pregnancy until the placenta takes over steroidogenesis.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes the hormonal trigger for ovulation?
o: A sustained low level of estrogen throughout the follicular phase
Direct stimulation by GnRH acting on the ovary
A surge in luteinizing hormone (LH), triggered by peak estrogen levels from the dominant follicle via positive feedback
A fall in FSH with no LH involvement
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: Sustained high estrogen from the mature dominant follicle switches from negative to positive feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, triggering the LH surge that induces ovulation approximately 36 hours later.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which epithelium lines the ectocervix (vaginal portion of the cervix)?
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The ectocervix is lined by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium, continuous with the vaginal epithelium, while the endocervical canal is lined by simple columnar mucus-secreting epithelium; their junction is the transformation zone.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes changes in cervical mucus around the time of ovulation?
o: It becomes thin, clear, watery, and elastic (increased spinnbarkeit), facilitating sperm penetration
It becomes thick and scant, forming a mucus plug
There is no cyclical change in cervical mucus
It becomes acidic and hostile to sperm
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: Rising estrogen around ovulation causes cervical mucus to become thin, clear, watery, and highly elastic (increased spinnbarkeit), facilitating sperm penetration and transport, in contrast to the thick, scant mucus of the luteal phase under progesterone influence.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which ligament provides the main support connecting the cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the pelvic side wall, and contains the uterine artery and vein?
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The cardinal (transverse cervical) ligaments extend from the cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the pelvic side wall, providing major structural support to the uterus and containing the uterine vessels.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which ligament contains the ovarian artery, vein, and nerves as they travel from the posterior abdominal wall to the ovary?
o: Suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament)
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament) carries the ovarian vessels and nerves from the posterior abdominal wall to the ovary, and is an important structure to identify during pelvic surgery to avoid ureteric injury.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes the arterial anastomosis clinically relevant to uterine blood supply during pregnancy and surgery?
o: The uterine artery arises directly from the aorta
The uterine artery anastomoses with the ovarian artery, providing collateral circulation to the uterus and ovary
The uterine artery anastomoses only with the vaginal artery, with no ovarian connection
The uterine artery has no anastomotic connections
The uterine artery is a branch of the external iliac artery
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The uterine artery (a branch of the internal iliac artery) anastomoses with the ovarian artery (a direct branch of the aorta) along the broad ligament, providing collateral blood supply important in pregnancy and pelvic surgery.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes the primordial follicle, the earliest stage of ovarian follicular development?
o: A follicle that has already completed meiosis II
The final stage of follicular development just before ovulation
An oocyte arrested in the diplotene stage of meiosis I, surrounded by a single layer of flattened granulosa (follicular) cells
A mature oocyte surrounded by multiple layers of cuboidal granulosa cells and an antral cavity
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The primordial follicle consists of a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I (diplotene stage) surrounded by a single layer of flattened (squamous) follicular/granulosa cells, representing the resting pool of oocytes present from before birth.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best explains why oocytes are arrested in meiosis I from before birth until just prior to ovulation?
o: Arrest occurs at metaphase II from birth, not prophase I
Meiosis is completed entirely before birth
Oocyte meiotic maturation inhibitor factors maintain meiotic arrest at the diplotene stage of prophase I until the LH surge triggers resumption of meiosis
Meiosis only begins at puberty, with no earlier initiation
Oocytes never undergo meiosis; only mitosis occurs
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: Oocytes enter meiosis I during fetal development but arrest at the diplotene stage of prophase I due to inhibitory factors within the follicle; this arrest persists until the preovulatory LH surge triggers resumption of meiosis I, with a second arrest at metaphase II until fertilization.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes the myometrium's structural composition and primary physiological role?
o: A thin serosal covering with no muscular component
The mucosal lining that is shed during menstruation
Simple columnar glandular epithelium responsible for secretion
A thick layer of smooth muscle that provides the contractile force for labor and menstruation
A layer composed purely of connective tissue with no muscle
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The myometrium is the thick middle layer of the uterine wall composed of smooth muscle, responsible for the powerful contractions of labor and for expelling menstrual debris.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes the vaginal epithelium's response to estrogen, relevant to cytological (e.g., Pap smear) assessment of hormonal status?
o: Progesterone, not estrogen, is the main determinant of vaginal maturation
Estrogen has no effect on vaginal epithelium
Vaginal epithelium is unresponsive to any sex steroid
Estrogen promotes maturation and glycogen accumulation in vaginal squamous epithelial cells, changes that can be assessed cytologically
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: Estrogen promotes proliferation, maturation, and glycogen accumulation within vaginal squamous epithelial cells; cytological assessment of maturation index can reflect estrogen status.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes the primary source of estrogen production within the ovarian follicle, according to the two-cell, two-gonadotropin theory?
o: Estrogen is produced exclusively by the adrenal cortex, not the ovary
Theca interna cells (LH-stimulated) produce androgens that diffuse to granulosa cells (FSH-stimulated), which aromatize them to estrogens
The corpus albicans is the primary estrogen source
Granulosa cells alone, with no theca cell contribution
Theca cells alone convert cholesterol directly to estrogen without granulosa involvement
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: According to the two-cell, two-gonadotropin theory, LH stimulates theca interna cells to produce androgens, which diffuse into adjacent granulosa cells; FSH stimulates granulosa cell aromatase activity, converting these androgens into estrogens.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes the anatomical relationship of the ureter to the uterine artery, a relationship of major surgical importance ("water under the bridge")?
o: The ureter passes through the substance of the uterus itself
The ureter passes inferior and posterior (deep) to the uterine artery near the lateral fornix of the vagina
The ureter passes anterior and superior to the uterine artery
The uterine artery passes through the ureter
The ureter and uterine artery never come into close proximity
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The ureter passes beneath (inferior and posterior to) the uterine artery near the lateral vaginal fornix and cervix — the classic "water under the bridge" relationship — making it vulnerable to injury during hysterectomy when the uterine artery is clamped.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes the round ligament of the uterus?
o: A fibromuscular cord that runs from the uterine cornu through the inguinal canal to the labia majora, providing minor anterior support to the uterus
A ligament containing the ovarian vessels
The main structural support of the uterus against prolapse
A ligament connecting the ovary to the pelvic wall
A remnant of the mesonephric duct in females
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The round ligament, a fibromuscular remnant of the gubernaculum, runs from the uterine cornu through the inguinal canal to insert into the labia majora, providing some anterior stabilization of the uterine fundus, though it is not a major weight-bearing support structure.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes the normal anatomical positioning of the uterus in most individuals?
o: Anteverted (tilted forward relative to the vaginal axis) and anteflexed (flexed forward relative to the cervix), though variation is common and usually normal
Positioned entirely within the abdominal cavity above the pelvic brim
Positioned vertically with no flexion or version
Retroverted and retroflexed in all individuals
Always fixed in a single position with no normal variation
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The uterus is typically anteverted and anteflexed, though anatomical variation (including retroversion) is common among healthy individuals and usually of no clinical significance on its own.

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.s: Which of the following best describes the histological composition of the ovarian cortex?
o: Colloid-filled follicles identical to thyroid follicles
Predominantly follicles at various stages of development embedded in a dense connective tissue stroma
A single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium
Predominantly blood vessels with no follicular structures
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.e: The ovarian cortex contains follicles at various developmental stages (primordial, primary, secondary, and mature) embedded within a dense, cellular connective tissue stroma, while the medulla centrally contains the main vascular and neural supply.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: The genetic sex of an embryo is determined at fertilization by which chromosomal combination?
o: Presence or absence of the Y chromosome (XY = male, XX = female)
The number of X chromosomes alone, regardless of Y
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Genetic sex is determined at fertilization by the sex chromosome contributed by the sperm; presence of a Y chromosome (carrying the SRY gene) directs male development.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: The SRY gene, located on the Y chromosome, initiates male gonadal development by directing the bipotential gonad to become which structure?
o: A testis, via differentiation of Sertoli and later Leydig cells
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: SRY (sex-determining region Y) triggers differentiation of the bipotential gonad into a testis, with subsequent Sertoli and Leydig cell development driving male phenotypic development.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: In the absence of the SRY gene and testis-determining factors, the bipotential gonad develops by default into which structure?
o: A structure identical to the adrenal cortex
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: In the absence of SRY and testicular differentiation signals, the bipotential gonad develops by default into an ovary, reflecting the historically termed 'default' female pathway of gonadal development.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: The paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts, in the presence of anti-Mullerian hormone from fetal Sertoli cells, undergo which fate?
o: Regress, preventing development of female internal genitalia in males
Persist unchanged with no functional significance
Persist and develop into the uterus and fallopian tubes
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH), secreted by fetal Sertoli cells, causes regression of the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts, preventing development of female internal structures (uterus, fallopian tubes, upper vagina) in males.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: In females, in the absence of anti-Mullerian hormone, the paramesonephric ducts develop into which structures?
o: Uterus, fallopian tubes, and upper vagina
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Without AMH-induced regression, the paramesonephric ducts persist and differentiate into the fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper portion of the vagina.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: The mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts, under the influence of testosterone from fetal Leydig cells, differentiate into which male internal genital structures?
o: Epididymis, vas deferens, and seminal vesicle
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Testosterone from fetal Leydig cells stimulates the ipsilateral mesonephric duct to differentiate into the epididymis, vas deferens, and seminal vesicle.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: External genitalia differentiation (male versus female phenotype) depends primarily on the presence or absence of which hormone, acting on the genital tubercle, folds, and swellings?
o: Dihydrotestosterone (DHT), converted from testosterone by 5-alpha reductase
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: DHT, formed from testosterone via 5-alpha reductase in genital tissue, drives virilization of the external genitalia (genital tubercle to glans penis, genital folds to penile shaft/scrotum), while its absence results in the default female external genitalia pattern.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes virilization of female external genitalia due to excess production of which hormone class?
o: Excess adrenal androgens (due to shunting of precursors away from blocked cortisol synthesis)
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: 21-hydroxylase deficiency impairs cortisol (and often aldosterone) synthesis, causing ACTH-driven overstimulation of the adrenal cortex and shunting of steroid precursors toward androgen synthesis, virilizing female fetuses.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Androgen insensitivity syndrome results from a defect in which receptor, causing a genetically male (XY) individual to develop a female external phenotype despite normal or elevated testosterone levels?
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Androgen insensitivity syndrome results from androgen receptor dysfunction, preventing target tissues from responding to testosterone/DHT, resulting in a female external phenotype in a genetically male (46,XY) individual, despite testes and normal/high testosterone.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: The placenta develops from which two components, fetal and maternal?
o: Only fetal tissue, with no maternal contribution
Fetal yolk sac and maternal endometrium exclusively
Only maternal tissue, with no fetal contribution
Fetal chorion frondosum and maternal decidua basalis
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: The definitive placenta forms from the fetal chorion frondosum (chorionic villi) interdigitating with the maternal decidua basalis.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), the hormone detected in pregnancy tests, is produced by which placental cell type?
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: The syncytiotrophoblast, the outer, invasive layer of the developing placenta, produces hCG, detectable in maternal blood/urine shortly after implantation.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which placental hormone, structurally similar to growth hormone, contributes to maternal insulin resistance during pregnancy, helping ensure adequate glucose supply to the fetus?
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Human placental lactogen (hPL) promotes maternal lipolysis and insulin resistance, increasing maternal blood glucose and free fatty acid availability to support fetal nutrition.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which hormone, produced by the placenta and detectable in maternal serum, is used as a marker of fetoplacental well-being, being synthesized via a pathway requiring both fetal adrenal and fetal liver contributions?
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Estriol synthesis requires precursor contributions from the fetal adrenal gland and fetal liver, in addition to placental enzymatic conversion, making it a marker reflecting both placental and fetal well-being.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Progesterone, essential for maintaining pregnancy, is initially produced by the corpus luteum and later, predominantly, by which structure?
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: After the first trimester, placental progesterone production (the 'luteal-placental shift') takes over from the corpus luteum, maintaining the pregnancy.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which hormone helps soften the cervix and relax pelvic ligaments in preparation for labor, produced by the corpus luteum and placenta?
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Relaxin, produced by the corpus luteum (and placenta), promotes cervical softening and relaxation of pelvic ligaments, facilitating parturition.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Parturition (labor onset) is a complex process, but which hormone's rising levels and receptor upregulation is critically important for triggering coordinated uterine contractions?
o: Oxytocin (with increasing myometrial oxytocin receptor density near term)
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: While multiple factors contribute to labor onset, rising myometrial oxytocin receptor density near term increases uterine sensitivity to oxytocin, contributing to the initiation and progression of coordinated contractions.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the fetal-to-maternal signal thought to help initiate the timing of parturition, involving the fetal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis?
o: Fetal cortisol production increases near term, contributing to a cascade of hormonal changes (including increased placental estrogen relative to progesterone) that promote labor onset
Maternal hormones alone, with no fetal contribution, determine labor timing
The fetus has no hormonal role in initiating labor
Fetal thyroid hormone is the primary trigger for labor
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Maturation of the fetal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, with increasing fetal cortisol production near term, is thought to contribute to a hormonal cascade (including changes in placental steroid production) that helps initiate the process of labor.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Twin pregnancies resulting from fertilization of two separate ova by two separate sperm are termed what, and what is their genetic relationship?
o: Dizygotic twins, genetically as similar as any siblings (non-identical)
Twins with identical genetic material regardless of fertilization pattern
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Dizygotic (fraternal) twins arise from separate fertilization of two ova by two sperm, making them genetically no more similar than typical siblings, unlike genetically identical monozygotic twins from a single zygote.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following describes the process and approximate timing by which monozygotic twins splitting very late (after approximately day 13) can result in a specific, high-risk anomaly?
o: Conjoined twins, due to incomplete separation of the embryonic disc
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Very late splitting of the embryonic disc (after approximately day 13, once the primitive streak has formed) can result in incomplete separation, producing conjoined twins.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes ectopic pregnancy, most commonly occurring in which anatomical location?
o: A normal variant of intrauterine pregnancy
Implantation outside the uterine cavity, most commonly in the ampulla of the fallopian tube
Implantation exclusively in the abdominal cavity
Implantation in the cervix in the majority of cases
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Ectopic pregnancy refers to implantation outside the normal uterine cavity location, most commonly within the fallopian tube (particularly the ampullary region), representing a significant cause of early pregnancy complications and hemorrhage.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the genetic determinant that initiates male gonadal differentiation in the developing embryo?
o: The absence of the Y chromosome
The presence of two X chromosomes
The SRY gene on the Y chromosome, which triggers testis-determining factor expression leading to testicular development
A gene located on the X chromosome exclusively
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: The SRY (sex-determining region Y) gene on the Y chromosome encodes testis-determining factor, which initiates differentiation of the bipotential gonad into a testis; in its absence, the gonad defaults toward ovarian development.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which embryonic duct system regresses in the male fetus due to anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) secreted by fetal Sertoli cells?
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Anti-Müllerian hormone, secreted by fetal Sertoli cells, causes regression of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts in male fetuses, which would otherwise develop into the uterus, uterine tubes, and upper vagina.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: In the female fetus, in the absence of anti-Müllerian hormone, which duct system persists and differentiates into the uterus, uterine tubes, and upper vagina?
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Without AMH (absent in female fetuses), the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts persist and differentiate into the uterine tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina, while the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts regress without testosterone support.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the role of fetal testosterone (and its metabolite dihydrotestosterone) in male external genital development?
o: Dihydrotestosterone acts only on the gonad, not external genitalia
Testosterone stimulates the mesonephric duct to form the epididymis, vas deferens, and seminal vesicles, while dihydrotestosterone drives differentiation of the external genitalia and prostate
Testosterone has no role in genital differentiation
Testosterone causes regression of the Wolffian duct
Estrogen alone determines male external genital development
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Testosterone from fetal Leydig cells stabilizes and stimulates the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct to differentiate into the epididymis, vas deferens, and seminal vesicles, while its 5-alpha-reduced metabolite dihydrotestosterone (DHT) drives virilization of the external genitalia and prostate.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the process of implantation of the blastocyst?
o: Implantation occurs immediately after fertilization within the uterine tube
Implantation never occurs within the endometrium, only the myometrium
Implantation is mediated entirely by the inner cell mass with no trophoblast involvement
Implantation always occurs within the cervix
The trophoblast invades the endometrium (typically the posterior or anterior wall of the uterine fundus), occurring approximately 6-10 days after fertilization
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Implantation occurs when the trophoblast of the blastocyst invades the endometrial lining, typically in the fundal region of the uterus, approximately 6-10 days after fertilization.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which structure differentiates into the syncytiotrophoblast and cytotrophoblast, layers responsible for hormone production and invasion during implantation?
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: The trophoblast, the outer cell layer of the blastocyst, differentiates into the invasive syncytiotrophoblast (hormone-secreting, including hCG) and the underlying proliferative cytotrophoblast, together forming the placenta's fetal component.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which hormone, secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast, forms the basis of standard pregnancy tests due to its early and rapid rise after implantation?
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: hCG is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast almost immediately after implantation, rising rapidly in early pregnancy, which is the basis for detecting pregnancy in blood and urine tests.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the role of human placental lactogen (hPL) during pregnancy?
o: It has no metabolic role during pregnancy
It is produced exclusively by the fetal liver
It promotes maternal lipolysis and insulin resistance, shifting maternal metabolism to favor glucose and amino acid availability for the fetus
It functions identically to hCG in maintaining the corpus luteum
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Human placental lactogen (hPL), produced by the syncytiotrophoblast, promotes maternal insulin resistance and lipolysis, sparing glucose and amino acids for fetal use, particularly important as pregnancy progresses.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: By which gestational timepoint does the placenta typically take over as the primary source of progesterone production, superseding the corpus luteum (the so-called luteal-placental shift)?
o: The corpus luteum remains the sole source of progesterone throughout pregnancy
Not until the third trimester (28 weeks)
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: The luteal-placental shift occurs around 8-10 weeks of gestation, when the placenta becomes capable of producing sufficient progesterone independently, after which the corpus luteum is no longer essential for pregnancy maintenance.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the germ layer origin of the gonads (excluding germ cells) and much of the reproductive tract?
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: The gonads develop from the intermediate mesoderm forming the urogenital ridge, alongside the developing kidney; primordial germ cells, in contrast, originate extragonadally (from the yolk sac wall) and migrate into the developing gonad.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the migratory origin of primordial germ cells before they colonize the developing gonad?
o: They originate in the neural crest and migrate ventrally
They originate in the allantois and migrate through the umbilical cord
They originate within the gonadal ridge itself and never migrate
They arise in the wall of the yolk sac and migrate along the dorsal mesentery to the developing gonadal ridge
They arise from the mesonephric duct directly
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Primordial germ cells originate extragonadally in the wall of the yolk sac near the allantois and migrate along the dorsal mesentery of the hindgut to colonize the developing gonadal ridge.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the placental barrier's classification and general permeability characteristics?
o: The placental barrier is impermeable to all substances including oxygen
There is no exchange of nutrients or gases across the human placenta

It is a hemochorial placenta in humans, where maternal blood directly bathes the chorionic villi, with selective permeability governed by villous membranes rather than a continuous maternal endothelium
The human placenta is epitheliochorial with six tissue layers separating maternal and fetal blood
Maternal and fetal blood mix freely with no barrier at all
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: The human placenta is hemochorial, meaning maternal blood directly bathes the chorionic villi (with no intervening maternal endothelium), while fetal blood remains within villous capillaries; exchange occurs across the syncytiotrophoblast and villous capillary wall, which selectively regulates transfer of nutrients, gases, and waste.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the source and role of relaxin during pregnancy and parturition?
o: It functions identically to oxytocin in stimulating uterine contraction
Produced mainly by the corpus luteum (and placenta), it helps relax pelvic ligaments and soften the cervix in preparation for delivery
It is produced solely by the fetal adrenal gland and has no maternal effect
It has no role in pregnancy physiology
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Relaxin, produced by the corpus luteum and later the placenta, promotes relaxation of pelvic ligaments and cervical softening (ripening), helping prepare the pelvis and cervix for parturition.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the fetal adrenal-placental cooperation (fetoplacental unit) required for estriol synthesis during pregnancy?
o: Estriol is synthesized entirely within the placenta with no fetal contribution
Estriol is synthesized entirely by the maternal ovary
Estriol synthesis requires only maternal cholesterol with no fetal enzymatic steps
The fetal adrenal gland produces DHEA-S, which is sulfated further by the fetal liver and then aromatized by the placenta into estriol
The fetal adrenal has no role in steroidogenesis during pregnancy
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Estriol synthesis during pregnancy depends on the fetoplacental unit: the fetal adrenal gland produces DHEA-S, which undergoes 16-hydroxylation in the fetal liver, and the placenta (lacking certain enzymes itself) aromatizes these precursors into estriol, making estriol a marker of fetoplacental well-being.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the physiological trigger classically proposed for the onset of labor involving prostaglandins and oxytocin?
o: Labor onset is entirely random with no hormonal correlation
Labor is triggered exclusively by fetal movement
Only progesterone withdrawal, with no role for prostaglandins or oxytocin
A sudden absence of all reproductive hormones
Rising prostaglandin synthesis (stimulating myometrial contractility and cervical ripening) combined with increased myometrial oxytocin receptor sensitivity near term
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: The onset of labor involves multiple coordinated changes, including increased prostaglandin synthesis promoting cervical ripening and myometrial contractility, along with upregulation of myometrial oxytocin receptors, increasing uterine sensitivity to oxytocin near term.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the embryological origin of the vaginal epithelium's lower portion, distinguishing it from the upper vagina's Müllerian origin?
o: The lower vagina develops from neural crest tissue
The entire vagina develops from the allantois
The upper and lower vagina share an identical urogenital sinus origin
The entire vagina develops solely from the mesonephric duct
The lower vagina develops from the urogenital sinus, while the upper vagina (and uterus, uterine tubes) develops from the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: The vagina has a dual embryological origin: the upper portion derives from the fused paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts, while the lower portion derives from the urogenital sinus, with the vaginal plate canalizing to form the vaginal lumen.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the significance of the genital tubercle in external genital development?
o: It develops exclusively into female external genitalia regardless of hormonal environment
It is a bipotential structure that develops into the glans penis in males (under androgen influence) or the clitoris in females (in the absence of androgen influence)
It has no role in external genital development
It differentiates only in male fetuses, with no female homolog
It develops into the labia majora only
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: The genital tubercle is a bipotential embryonic structure: under the influence of dihydrotestosterone it elongates to form the glans penis, whereas in its absence it forms the clitoris, illustrating the shared embryological origin of homologous male and female structures.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes decidualization of the endometrium in the context of implantation?
o: Transformation of the myometrium into a secretory structure
Progesterone-driven transformation of endometrial stromal cells into specialized decidual cells that support and regulate trophoblast invasion
A process that occurs only after delivery
A process independent of any hormonal influence
Complete degeneration of the endometrium with no further function
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Decidualization is the progesterone-dependent transformation of endometrial stromal cells into decidual cells, which occurs in preparation for and during implantation, providing a nutritive and immunologically regulated environment for the invading trophoblast.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the physiological reason maternal thyroid hormone requirements increase during pregnancy?
o: Pregnancy has no effect on thyroid physiology
Only free thyroid hormone changes, with no effect on binding proteins
The placenta produces sufficient thyroid hormone independently, eliminating maternal thyroid contribution
Thyroid hormone requirements decrease during pregnancy
Increased hepatic synthesis of thyroxine-binding globulin (driven by estrogen) increases total bound thyroid hormone requirements, plus increased metabolic demand and placental hormone degradation
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: Estrogen-driven increases in hepatic thyroxine-binding globulin synthesis raise total thyroid hormone requirements during pregnancy, and increased metabolic demands along with placental deiodinase activity further increase maternal thyroid hormone needs.

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.s: Which of the following best describes the fate of most primordial germ cells in the female fetus following their arrival in the developing ovary?
o: They migrate out of the gonad permanently
They differentiate directly into granulosa cells
They undergo meiosis II completion before birth
They remain as germ cells without ever entering meiosis until after menopause
They undergo mitotic proliferation (oogonia) followed by entry into meiosis I, becoming primary oocytes that arrest in prophase I before birth
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.e: After colonizing the ovary, primordial germ cells (oogonia) proliferate mitotically, then enter meiosis I as primary oocytes, arresting in the diplotene stage of prophase I before birth, where most remain until stimulated to resume meiosis around ovulation, potentially decades later.
